topic: Compute matrix chain multiplication.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Walk me through the dynamic programming solution for Matrix Chain Multiplication: how you define the DP state, the recurrence, and how you reconstruct the optimal parenthesization from the DP tables. Also mention the time and space complexity and why the greedy “always multiply the smallest dimensions first” strategy fails here.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for the dynamic programming solution, I’d define the DP state as something like dp[i][j] being the minimum cost to multiply the i-th matrix with the j-th matrix in the chain. The recurrence would be:

dp[i][j] = min over k from i to j-1 of (dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + cost of multiplying those two resulting matrices).

To reconstruct the parenthesization, we usually keep another table, say split[i][j], that stores which k gave the minimum cost, and then we recursively print the parentheses from that.

For complexity, both time and space are O(n^2), since we’re filling an n by n table and for each cell we do a constant amount of work based on precomputed results. The greedy idea of always picking the smallest dimensions first doesn’t work because choosing a locally minimal multiplication might force very large intermediate matrices later, but the DP guarantees a globally optimal solution.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good structure overall, but note the time complexity is actually O(n^3) because for each of the O(n^2) (i, j) pairs you iterate over all k between them. To probe your understanding: how would you implement a top-down (memoized) version of Matrix Chain Multiplication, and what are the pros and cons of top-down vs bottom-up DP in this specific problem?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, that makes sense on the O(n^3).

For a top-down version, I’d write a recursive function solve(i, j) that returns the minimum cost to multiply matrices i..j. Base case: if i == j, cost is 0. Otherwise:

solve(i, j) = min over k in [i, j-1] of:
  solve(i, k) + solve(k+1, j) + p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j]

I’d memoize results in a 2D array dp[i][j], initialized to some sentinel (like -1), and only recurse if dp[i][j] isn’t already computed. Optionally, I’d have a split[i][j] table to remember the best k for reconstruction.

Pros of top-down here: easier to write and reason about, and it only computes states that are actually needed. Bottom-up pros: no recursion overhead, predictable iteration order, and often better cache behavior; for MCM, we typically know we’ll need almost all dp[i][j], so bottom-up is usually preferred in practice.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Let’s tweak the problem: suppose instead of minimizing the total number of scalar multiplications, you want to minimize the maximum size (in terms of number of elements) of any intermediate matrix generated during the chain multiplication; how would you redefine the DP state and recurrence, and how would the complexity compare to the classic MCM solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, let me just clarify what you mean by “size” here. Are we measuring size as the total number of elements in the intermediate matrix (i.e., rows × columns), and the objective is to minimize the maximum such value over the whole sequence of multiplications, regardless of the total scalar multiplications?  

Also, do we still assume the result must be the fully multiplied single matrix at the end, or are we just optimizing the sequence under that new objective?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions; you understood it correctly: size is rows × columns of any intermediate matrix, and we still must end with the single fully multiplied result. With that in mind, how would you set up the DP to minimize the maximum intermediate matrix size instead of total scalar multiplications, and what would the recurrence and overall time complexity look like compared to classic MCM?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d keep almost the same DP structure, but change what dp[i][j] represents and how we combine subproblems.

Let dp[i][j] be the minimum possible “maximum intermediate size” (rows × cols) that can appear when multiplying matrices i..j into one matrix. The final matrix shape for i..j is still fixed by the dimensions array p[], so matrix i..j always has dimensions p[i-1] × p[j], regardless of parenthesization.

The recurrence would be:

dp[i][i] = p[i-1] * p[i]   // the size of the i-th matrix itself

For i < j:

dp[i][j] = min over k in [i, j-1] of:
    max( dp[i][k],
         dp[k+1][j],
         p[i-1] * p[j] )   // the size of the resulting matrix from multiplying (i..k) × (k+1..j)

We’re taking, for each split, the worst (maximum) intermediate size seen in the left part, the right part, and the final product at that split, and then choosing the split that minimizes that worst-case.

Complexity-wise, it’s the same as classic MCM: O(n^3) time (O(n^2) states, O(n) splits per state) and O(n^2) space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and nicely adapted to the new objective; the DP structure and complexity are correct. Let’s wrap on a conceptual one: can you explain why Matrix Chain Multiplication is a good example of optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems, and contrast it with a parenthesization-like problem where optimal substructure fails (so the DP approach would not work as cleanly)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, let me make sure I understand what you’re looking for. 

For the contrast part, do you want an example that’s still about putting parentheses in some expression, but where the “best way” to parenthesize the whole thing doesn’t necessarily use the best parenthesizations of the subexpressions? Like, are you thinking of something with extra global constraints or context (e.g., precedence, non-associative operators, or side effects), or just any problem where local optimal choices for subchains don’t compose into a global optimum?

topic: Check if two strings are anagrams of each other.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you check if two strings are anagrams of each other? Walk me through at least two different approaches, discuss their time and space complexity, and mention any edge cases you’d watch out for (like Unicode, case, or very long strings).

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so first approach: if we can sort, I’d normalize both strings (e.g., same case, maybe strip spaces if that’s in the spec), then if their lengths differ, return false. Otherwise sort both strings and compare them. Sorting is O(n log n) time and O(1) or O(n) extra space depending on the sort implementation.

Second approach: use a frequency count. Again, normalize and check lengths first. Then iterate over the first string and increment counts for each character in a hash map (or fixed-size array if we know the charset), then iterate over the second string and decrement. If we ever see a character not present or a count goes negative, it’s not an anagram; at the end, all counts should be zero. This is O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the charset size.

For edge cases, I’d clarify how to treat case (e.g., “A” vs “a”), whether to ignore spaces and punctuation, and how to handle Unicode combining characters and normalization (NFC vs NFD), since visually identical strings might not be byte-for-byte the same. For very long strings, I’d prefer the counting approach to avoid the O(n log n) sort cost.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you hit all the right trade-offs. Now, suppose you have a huge stream of characters coming in (potentially unbounded), and you want to check, at any given time, if the last k characters in the stream form an anagram of a given pattern string P of length k; how would you design this to run efficiently, and what would the time and space complexity look like?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me make sure I understand the setup. Are we talking about a continuous online scenario where characters keep arriving one by one, and after each new character I should be able to say “yes/no, the last k chars form an anagram of P”? And is k fixed and equal to |P|, or can k change over time?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions – your understanding is correct: characters arrive one by one in an online fashion, after each arrival you should be able to say whether the last k characters form an anagram of a fixed pattern P, and k = |P| is fixed. How would you design this so each new character can be processed efficiently, and what are the time and space complexities per character and overall?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so since the stream can be huge, I’d avoid storing the whole thing and just keep track of global character frequencies seen so far, and compare that against the pattern P’s frequency map.

I’d precompute a frequency map for P once. Then, as each new character arrives from the stream, I’d update a running frequency map for all characters seen so far and check if that map matches P’s map; if they match, I’d say the last k characters form an anagram of P. With a fixed alphabet, each update/check is basically O(1) time per character, and space is O(1) for the two frequency arrays.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: This is slightly misunderstood: we only care about the last k characters, not the entire stream’s global frequency. How would you maintain a sliding window of size k over the stream so that after each new character you can tell if that window is an anagram of P, and what update operations would you do when a character enters and when one leaves the window?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, got it, so I’ll keep a sliding window but I’m thinking of it as “up to size k” rather than exactly k.

I’d maintain a queue (or ring buffer) of the recent characters and a frequency map for that window. For each new character, I push it into the queue, increment its count, and then check if the current window’s frequency matches P’s frequencies; if the queue size ever exceeds k, I’ll just clear the whole window and start over from this new character, so I don’t have to worry about removing individual counts. Comparing the two frequency maps each time is O(1) with a fixed alphabet, and space is O(k) for the window plus O(1) for the maps.

topic: Find minimum cost path in a 2D grid.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you have an N x M grid where each cell has a non-negative cost, and you start at (0,0) and want to reach (N-1,M-1) moving only right or down. How would you compute the minimum cost path, and what time and space complexity would your approach have?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d probably use a greedy approach here. Starting from (0,0), at each step I would look at the two possible moves (right and down), compare their immediate cell costs, and always move to the smaller one. I’d repeat that until I reach (N-1, M-1), summing up the costs along the way, and that sum would be my minimum path cost.  

Right, so I guess the time complexity would be O(N + M) since I only take exactly N-1 downs and M-1 rights, and the space complexity would be O(1) because I’m not storing any extra data structures apart from a few variables.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear but the approach is actually wrong, since a locally cheapest move can block a globally optimal path. Can you think of a dynamic programming formulation for this problem: define the DP state, the recurrence relation, and how you would implement it iteratively to get the minimum cost?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for dynamic programming I’d define dp[i][j] as just the cost of the cell (i, j) itself, not the path cost to reach it. Then the recurrence would be something like: dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) without adding the current grid cost, because we already stored the cell’s cost there.

For the first row and first column, I’d just copy the grid values directly since there’s only one way to get there. Then I’d fill the dp table row by row using that recurrence, and in the end, dp[N-1][M-1] would give me the minimum path cost. Time complexity would be O(N*M) and space complexity would also be O(N*M).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your DP explanation was clear but the recurrence is wrong because dp[i][j] must represent the best path cost to reach (i, j), not just the cell cost. Let’s change gears: suppose you now can move right, down, or diagonally down-right on the same cost grid; how would you adapt your algorithm to handle this new move while still finding the minimum-cost path and what changes in the complexity, if any?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so if we add a diagonal move, I actually think we can go back to a greedy strategy and it’ll still work. From each cell, I’d just look at the three neighbors: right, down, and diagonal, and always pick the one with the smallest immediate cost. Since diagonal kind of “skips” both a right and a down, it should naturally give us the best shortcut when it’s cheaper.

So I’d follow that until I hit the bottom-right. The number of steps is still proportional to N + M because I’m shrinking either the row, the column, or both each move, so I’d say time complexity is O(N + M) and space is O(1), same idea as before.

topic: Find longest common prefix among a list of strings.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you’re given an array of N strings; how would you find their longest common prefix in an efficient way, and what is the time complexity in terms of N and the average string length L?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the straightforward way is vertical scanning. I’d first handle edge cases like an empty array. Then I’d take the first string as a reference and for each character position i, compare that character with the character at position i in every other string. As soon as I either reach the end of one string or find a mismatch at some position, I stop and return the prefix up to i.  

This runs in O(N * L), where N is the number of strings and L is the length of the longest common prefix (bounded by average string length). Space complexity is O(1) extra, ignoring the output string.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Suppose these strings are very long and numerous; can you describe an alternative approach using a trie, and compare its time and space complexity to your vertical scanning method?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so with a trie, I’d insert all N strings character by character. Each node has up to 26 (or alphabet-size) children and a count or end-of-word flag. To get the longest common prefix, I start from the root and walk down as long as the current node has exactly one child and is not the end of a word; the path I traverse is the prefix.

Building the trie takes O(total characters) = O(N * L). Extracting the prefix is at most O(L). So time is similar to vertical scanning in big-O, but the constant factors and space are worse: space is O(N * L) for all nodes. The benefit is it can be more efficient if I later need other prefix operations, but just for LCP, vertical scan is usually simpler and more space-efficient.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and well-balanced. Now imagine the strings are coming in as a stream, one by one, and after each insertion you need to be able to report the current longest common prefix of all strings seen so far; how would you maintain and update the LCP efficiently as each new string arrives, and what would be the per-string update complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Let me think… so I’d just maintain the current LCP string as I go. When a new string arrives, I compare it with the current LCP character by character and shorten the LCP to the common part. If at some point they differ at position i, I cut the LCP to length i; if there’s no common prefix, LCP becomes empty.  

The per-string update cost is O(L), where L is the length of the current LCP or the new string (whichever is smaller). Space is just storing that LCP plus the new string.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That streaming update approach was clear and correct. As a twist, suppose you’re given two very long strings (say up to 10^7 characters each) and you need to find their longest common prefix but accessing characters is relatively expensive (e.g., over a network); can you think of a way to reduce the number of character comparisons, and discuss trade-offs compared to the straightforward linear scan?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if character access itself is expensive, I’d try to batch the work by prefetching chunks of the strings locally and then doing a normal linear scan on those chunks.

For example, I could request the first, say, 1 KB of both strings, compare them locally, and if they’re equal, then request the next 1 KB, and so on. If I hit a mismatch inside a chunk, I can then do a small binary search within that chunk to find the exact mismatch position while still working from local memory.

This way, the number of remote accesses is reduced to O(L / chunkSize), where L is the LCP length, instead of one access per character. The trade-off is that I might transfer a bit more data than strictly needed if the mismatch occurs early in a chunk, but in terms of remote calls I’ve reduced the overhead compared to a naive per-character scan.

topic: Add two numbers represented as linked lists.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you have two non-empty singly linked lists representing two non-negative integers, where each node contains a single digit and the digits are stored in reverse order (1’s place at the head). How would you add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list, and what’s the time and space complexity of your approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so we traverse both lists simultaneously, digit by digit. We maintain a carry and a dummy head for the result list. At each step, we read the current digit from each list (or 0 if that list is exhausted), compute sum = x + y + carry, set the new digit as sum % 10, and update carry = sum / 10. We append the new node to the result list and advance the pointers. At the end, if carry is non-zero, we add a final node. Time complexity is O(m + n) since we visit each node once, and space complexity is O(m + n) for the new linked list we create.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the digits are stored in forward order (most significant digit at the head) and you are not allowed to reverse the lists; how would you add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify one constraint. When you say I’m not allowed to reverse the lists, do you mean no in-place reversal of the original lists, but I can still use auxiliary data structures like stacks or recursion? Or are you expecting an approach that doesn’t conceptually reverse the order at all?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question – assume you can’t modify or reverse the original lists in-place, but you may use auxiliary data structures (like stacks or recursion) as long as the overall solution is efficient. With that in mind, how would you add two numbers when the digits are stored in forward order and return the sum as a linked list, and what are the time and space complexities?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Okay, got it that I can use extra space. One thing I want to confirm: are the two lists guaranteed to have no leading zeros (except maybe the number 0 itself), and can their lengths be different? Also, do you care if the extra space is O(m + n), or are you looking for something closer to O(1) auxiliary space?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Those are good questions. Yes, the lists can have different lengths, and you can assume no leading zeros except for the number 0 itself; O(m + n) extra space is fine. With that clarified, how would you add the two numbers stored in forward order without reversing the lists in-place, and what are the time and space complexities of your approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d use two stacks. I traverse each list once, push all digits of list1 onto stack1 and all digits of list2 onto stack2. Then I pop from both stacks, adding digits plus a carry, just like normal addition from least significant side: sum = a + b + carry, create a new node with sum % 10, update carry = sum / 10. 

To build the result in forward order, I keep prepending each new node to the head of the result list (so the most recent computed digit becomes the new head). At the end, if there’s a remaining carry, I create a new head node for it. Time complexity is O(m + n) for the traversals and additions, and space complexity is O(m + n) for the stacks and the output list.

topic: Rotate a 2D matrix by 90 degrees.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you rotate an n x n 2D matrix by 90 degrees clockwise in-place, without using any extra matrix? Briefly describe the core idea and the time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so the standard in-place way is: first transpose the matrix, then reverse each row.

Transpose means swap elements at (i, j) with (j, i) for all i < j. After that, for each row, reverse the elements in-place. That effectively rotates the matrix 90 degrees clockwise.

Time complexity is O(n²) since we touch each element a constant number of times, and space complexity is O(1) because we only do swaps within the same matrix.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now, how would you handle rotating a non-square matrix (m x n) by 90 degrees clockwise, and would it still be possible to do it fully in-place without extra space? Explain the key idea and any constraints you see.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for an m x n matrix, a 90-degree clockwise rotation gives you an n x m matrix, so the shape changes.

If I’m allowed to use extra space, I’d create a new n x m matrix and set out[j][m - 1 - i] = in[i][j]. Time is O(mn), space is O(mn).

If I must do it “in-place” in the strict sense (same buffer and no extra matrix), that’s generally not possible when m ≠ n because the layout size/shape changes. You could maybe do something if the matrix is stored in a 1D buffer and you allow element reordering with some constant extra variables, but that’s really more of a different representation; for a normal 2D array with fixed dimensions, true in-place rotation for non-square isn’t feasible.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you correctly called out the shape-change constraint. Suppose you must rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place, but you are not allowed to use the transpose-then-reverse trick; describe how you’d do it by rotating elements layer by layer in cycles of four, and outline the indices you would touch for one such 4-element cycle.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so you’re asking about a different way than transpose-then-reverse, but still kind of doing a similar two-step, I think.

What I’d do is process the matrix row by row and for each row i, I’d rotate it into the correct column j directly. So instead of doing a full transpose first, I’d compute the target position for each element (i, j) as (j, n - 1 - i) and swap them pairwise.

I’d go through only half the matrix to avoid double-swapping, something like iterating i from 0 to n - 1 and j from 0 to n / 2 - 1, and then swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][n - 1 - i]. That way I’m still doing the 90-degree rotation in-place, but more “directly” without explicitly thinking in terms of layers.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: You slightly misunderstood what I was asking for there; I meant the classic layer-by-layer 4-way swap approach. For a single layer, can you describe how you’d iterate over the outer ring and, for a given offset k, which four indices you’d move in a cycle when rotating 90 degrees clockwise? Please give the index pattern in terms of top, bottom, left, right, and k.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Ah, got it, layer-by-layer ring rotation.

For a given layer, I’d define:
top = layer
bottom = n - 1 - layer
left = layer
right = n - 1 - layer

Then for each offset k from 0 to right - left - 1, the 4-way cycle (for clockwise rotation) is:

1) top row, moving to right column:
   (top, left + k)

2) left column, moving to bottom row:
   (bottom - k, left)

3) bottom row, moving to right column:
   (bottom, right - k)

4) right column, moving to top row:
   (top + k, right)

And I’d rotate those four values in a cycle using a temp variable.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you’ve got the layer-based idea down. As a final twist: suppose the matrix is extremely large and stored on disk (or in paged memory) so you cannot load it all into RAM at once; conceptually, how would you adapt your 90-degree rotation approach to work in a block-wise or streaming fashion, and what are the main trade-offs you’d worry about (I/O, locality, complexity)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, let me make sure I understand the constraints correctly. When you say the matrix is stored on disk and too large for RAM, are we imagining that I can still read and write fixed-size blocks (say B x B submatrices) into memory, and I’m allowed multiple passes over the file?

Also, are you more interested in a high-level strategy for how to schedule these block reads/writes to simulate the same 90-degree rotation, or do you want me to worry about a concrete storage layout on disk (row-major file, tiled format, etc.)?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions. Yes, assume it’s stored row-major on disk, you can read/write fixed-size B x B tiles into RAM, and you can do multiple passes; focus on a high-level strategy for rotating using these tiles and briefly call out the main trade-offs in terms of I/O and complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, that makes sense. Conceptually, I’d treat the big matrix as a grid of B x B tiles instead of individual cells, and then rotate those tiles using the same “transpose + reverse rows” idea, but at tile granularity.

First, I’d do a tile-level transpose: for each tile (Ti,j) above the diagonal, I’d read Ti,j and Tj,i into memory (maybe one at a time with a temp buffer) and swap their contents on disk. Then I’d do a tile-level row reversal: for each tile in row i, I’d swap tile (i, j) with tile (i, nTiles - 1 - j). Inside each tile, I can do the usual in-memory rotation or just leave the tile contents as-is if I’m only doing tile transpose + row-reverse.

Main trade-offs: a lot of random I/O if tiles are small or poorly aligned, more passes over the data, and higher implementation complexity to manage tile indices and buffering. The benefit is bounded memory usage (O(B²)) and better locality if B is chosen to match the page/cache sizes.

topic: Given two integers, compute sum without using '+' or '-' (bitwise).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you compute the sum of two 32-bit signed integers using only bitwise operations, without using '+' or '-'? Please walk me through the core idea and explain what role XOR and AND each play in your solution.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify one thing. Are you expecting a solution that repeatedly applies bitwise operations in a loop until there’s no carry left, or are you more interested in a single-step expression that conceptually shows how XOR and AND combine to form the sum?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That’s a clear question, thanks. I’m looking for the iterative version: repeatedly using bitwise operations until there is no carry left, and I want you to explain the intuition of why XOR represents the partial sum and AND (with a shift) represents the carry. Can you now describe the algorithm step by step and then give its time complexity in terms of bit-width?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Okay, let me make sure I understand what you want in terms of detail. Do you want me to walk through the algorithm at the bit level with a small concrete example, like adding 5 and 3 in binary, or is a higher-level description of the loop (using XOR for sum, AND+shift for carry, repeat until carry is zero) enough, as long as I then state the time complexity in terms of the number of bits?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your question is clear and shows you’re thinking about the right level of detail. Let’s do this: first give me the high-level loop description (XOR for partial sum, AND+shift for carry, repeat until no carry), and then briefly illustrate it with a tiny example like adding 1 and 2 in binary so I can see you understand it concretely. Also, tell me how many iterations this might take in terms of the number of bits.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so the high-level loop is:

We keep two integers, say a and b. While b is not zero, we do:
1) Compute the partial sum without carry: sum = a XOR b. This adds the bits where they differ but ignores carries.
2) Compute the carry: carry = (a AND b) << 1. AND finds positions where both have 1s (where a carry should be generated), and shifting left by 1 moves that carry into the next higher bit.
3) Set a = sum and b = carry, and repeat until carry (b) becomes zero. At that point, a holds the final sum.

For a concrete example, adding 1 and 2:
1 is 01, 2 is 10.
sum = 01 XOR 10 = 11 (which is 3),
carry = (01 AND 10) << 1 = 00 << 1 = 00,
so carry is zero and we’re done; the result is 3.

In terms of time complexity with respect to bit-width, for fixed-width integers (like 32-bit), this converges in O(1) iterations in practice, but more generally you can think of it as O(k), where k is the number of bits, because in the worst case carries can propagate across the entire word.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on, including the complexity argument. As a follow-up, how does this bitwise addition behave with negative numbers in two’s complement, and are there any overflow edge cases you’d be careful about if you had to implement a function `int add(int a, int b)` using this approach in a language like C++ or Java?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so with two’s complement, this bitwise method still works for negative numbers because the hardware addition it’s mimicking is exactly two’s complement addition. XOR and AND don’t “care” about sign; they just operate on bits, and the representation handles the sign for us.

In C++ or Java with 32-bit ints, the behavior on overflow is the same as normal integer addition: you’ll wrap around modulo 2³². The algorithm won’t detect overflow by itself; it just produces the wrapped result. If I needed to detect signed overflow, I’d add an extra check, like seeing when a and b have the same sign but the result’s sign differs.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for regarding two’s complement and overflow behavior. Let’s zoom out a bit: if you had to generalize this idea to implement addition on arbitrarily large integers (bignums) represented as arrays or vectors of machine words, how would you structure that algorithm, and how would its time and space complexity compare to built-in integer addition?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for big integers stored as an array of words (say 32- or 64-bit chunks), I’d basically do what hardware does but at the word level.

I’d iterate from least significant word to most significant, adding corresponding words plus a carry word. The “addition” of two words could itself use the bitwise XOR/AND+shift loop we discussed, or just the built-in + on that word type. I’d store each result word in an output array, and propagate the carry to the next word; if there’s a leftover carry at the end, I’d append a new word.

Time complexity is O(n) where n is the number of words (i.e., proportional to the bit-length), and space is also O(n), maybe O(n+1) if I need an extra word for final carry. Compared to built-in fixed-width addition, which is O(1) at the language level, big-int addition is linear in the size of the number.

topic: Implement Kth largest element using a min-heap.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you maintain the kth largest element in a stream of numbers using a min-heap, and what would be the time and space complexity for both initialization with N elements and each new incoming element?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, just to clarify: when you say “maintain the kth largest element in a stream,” do you mean the data structure should support two phases — first being initialized with an existing array of N elements, and then handling one element at a time as they arrive? And for the complexities, do you want separate bounds for the initial build step versus the per-element update when a new number comes in?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarification question – your understanding is clear. Yes, assume two phases: first you’re given an initial array of N elements and a value k, then you receive elements one by one as a stream. Describe the data structure and operations you’d use with a min-heap, and give the time and space complexity for: 1) building from the initial N elements, and 2) processing each new incoming element.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d use a min-heap that stores all the elements we’ve seen so far. During initialization with N elements, I’d just insert all N elements into the min-heap, so that’s O(N log N) time and O(N) space. Then, to get the kth largest, I’d pop from the min-heap k times to reach the kth largest element, which would be O(k log N) per query.

For the stream part, every time a new element comes in, I’d just push it into the same min-heap in O(log N), and then again pop k times when I need the kth largest, which would still be O(k log N) per update. Space stays O(N) since we’re keeping all elements.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear but the approach is not optimal, because popping k times on every query defeats the purpose; with a min-heap, we usually want O(log k) per update and O(1) per query by keeping only k elements. Let me narrow it down: if you are allowed to store at most k elements in your min-heap at any time, how exactly would you handle (a) building from the initial N elements, and (b) processing each new incoming element, so that you can always return the kth largest in O(1)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I’m only allowed to store k elements in the min-heap, I’d just take the first k elements from the initial N, push them all into the heap, and then stop — that gives me a heap of size k in O(k log k). I don’t need to look at the remaining N − k elements, because the kth largest must be among the first k I saw.

Then for the stream, whenever a new element comes in, I compare it with the top of the min-heap. If it’s smaller than the top, I push it into the heap and pop the current top to keep the size at k. If it’s larger, I ignore it, since it can’t affect the kth largest. That way each update is O(log k), and the kth largest is always just the root in O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your reasoning is clear, but the logic is flipped: to maintain the kth largest with a min-heap of size k, you must consider all N elements initially, and in the stream you should only keep numbers that are at least as large as the current kth largest (the heap top), not discard larger ones. Let’s shift slightly: suppose you’ve correctly implemented this kth-largest-with-min-heap structure; how would you adapt the idea to maintain the kth smallest element in a stream, and what changes (if any) in your choice of heap type, comparisons, and complexities?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I think for kth smallest we can pretty much mirror what you just described, but still using a min-heap. Instead of tracking the largest elements, we now track the smallest ones, so I’d again keep a min-heap of size k, but this time it would contain the k smallest elements seen so far, and the root would be the smallest, which is also the kth smallest overall.

On initialization, I’d go through all N elements, push into the heap until I have k, and then for each remaining element, if it’s smaller than the heap top, I insert it and pop one to keep the size at k. For the stream, whenever a new number comes in, if it’s smaller than the heap top (current kth smallest), I push it and pop the largest from the heap. I think the complexities stay the same: O(N log k) to build and O(log k) per new element, and O(1) to read the kth smallest from the root.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: This is a bit mixed up: for kth largest we keep the k largest elements in a min-heap; for kth smallest we’d symmetrically keep the k smallest in a max-heap, so your heap choice and comparisons matter. Let’s zoom out: can you summarize, in your own words, the general pattern for when you’d pick a min-heap vs a max-heap to maintain an order statistic like “kth largest/smallest” in a stream, and how the heap size relates to k in each case?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so the general pattern I’d follow is: if I care about “largest” things, I pick a max-heap, and if I care about “smallest” things, I pick a min-heap. So for kth largest, I’d use a max-heap of size k that stores the k largest elements, and the root would be the kth largest because it’s the maximum among them. For kth smallest, I’d do the opposite: use a min-heap of size k that stores the k smallest elements, and the root would be the kth smallest.

In both cases, the heap size is always k, and whenever a new element comes in, if it should be among those k interesting elements (larger for kth largest, smaller for kth smallest), I push it and pop one to keep size k. That way the root always directly gives me the kth statistic I care about.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Thanks, I think we’ve explored this pattern enough; your answers were generally clear but had some conceptual mistakes around when to use min- vs max-heaps and what the heap root represents. Let’s wrap up here – I’d recommend revisiting kth largest/smallest with heaps and order statistics in streams as a follow-up practice topic.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, sorry, just to check — are we still talking about the heaps/order-statistic topic, or are you actually wrapping up the interview here? I wasn’t sure if you wanted me to correct my mental model about min-heap vs max-heap one more time, or if that was more of a final comment and we’re done.

topic: Solve partition equal subset sum.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you approach the Partition Equal Subset Sum problem: given a set of positive integers, determine if it can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sum? First describe the high-level idea, then walk me through a concrete algorithm and its time/space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so, first I’d note that if the total sum of the array is odd, it’s impossible, so we return false. If it’s even, say total = 2 * target, the problem becomes: can we find a subset that sums to target?

A standard way is using DP for subset sum. Let n be the number of elements and target = total / 2. We create a boolean DP array of size target + 1 where dp[s] means “can we form sum s.” Initialize dp[0] = true. Then for each number num in the array, we iterate s from target down to num and set dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num]. At the end, if dp[target] is true, we can partition; otherwise we can’t.

Time complexity is O(n * target), and space complexity is O(target) due to the 1D DP optimization.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now suppose the integers can be negative as well as positive; how does this affect your DP approach, and how would you adapt (or replace) it to still decide whether you can partition into two equal-sum subsets?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify the setting. When you say the integers can be negative as well as positive, are we still talking about a multiset of integers where we can only choose to include or exclude each number once, and we want to split the array into two disjoint subsets whose sums are exactly equal? Or are you also allowing multiple uses of the same number or any other constraints I should be aware of?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question – yes, it’s still a multiset, each element can be used at most once, and we just want to split into two disjoint subsets with equal sum. Given that, how would you adapt your DP (or choose a different data structure/approach) to handle negative numbers efficiently, and what would the new time and space complexities look like?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so with negatives, the simple 0..target DP array doesn’t work because sums can be negative and we don’t have a small fixed range around 0 in general.

If the range of possible sums is still reasonably bounded, one way is to track all reachable sums using an offset. For example, compute minSum and maxSum (sums of all negative and all positive numbers), then create a boolean DP array from [minSum..maxSum] with an offset. Initialize dp[0 + offset] = true, and for each num, update reachable sums similarly to before, iterating over the whole range and shifting by num. At the end, you check if totalSum is even and if totalSum / 2 is reachable.

Time and space would be O(n * (maxSum - minSum)), which can be large. If the range is too big, this becomes impractical and the problem is essentially NP-hard, so you’d need to fall back to something like a backtracking / meet-in-the-middle approach with exponential worst case instead of a clean pseudo-polynomial DP.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you correctly called out the pseudo-polynomial vs NP-hard aspect. As a follow-up, suppose the input size n is up to 200 and all numbers are positive but can be as large as 10^9; how would you change your approach to still solve Partition Equal Subset Sum within reasonable time, and what tradeoffs or pruning strategies would you rely on?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so with n up to 200 and values up to 1e9, the sum can be huge, so the classic sum-based DP is dead.

I’d switch to a state-based approach where the complexity depends more on n than on the sum. One practical way is to maintain a set (or sorted vector) of reachable sums and keep it pruned. Start with {0}, and for each num, generate new sums s + num from the current set, merge them in, and then prune dominated sums. For pruning, you can keep the reachable sums sorted and periodically remove sums that are “too close” to each other relative to the total, or cap the size of the set by discarding sums that are obviously far from total/2. The idea is to keep only a representative subset of sums that reasonably covers the range.

Another option is meet-in-the-middle: split the array into two halves of size ~100, enumerate all subset sums for each half (2^100 is too big, but with pruning or only keeping near-total/2 sums, you reduce), then try to combine sums from both sides to hit total/2. In both strategies, you rely on pruning/approximation to keep the number of tracked sums manageable, trading exact pseudo-polynomial guarantees for a heuristic but efficient solution in practice.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your last answer mixed in some heuristic/pruning ideas, which are interesting but drift away from a clean, exact algorithmic guarantee for this classic problem. Let’s zoom back to the standard setting: all numbers are positive and total sum is not too large; can you code (in words, not syntax) the 1D DP solution for Partition Equal Subset Sum, and explain any edge cases you’d be careful about while implementing it in a language like C++ or Java?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so in words, I’d do something like this:

First, compute the total sum. If total is odd, immediately return false. Let target = total / 2. Then create a boolean array dp of size target + 1, initialized to false. Set dp[0] = true because sum 0 is always achievable (empty subset).

Then iterate over each number num in the input array. For each num, loop s from target down to num, and set dp[s] = dp[s] OR dp[s - num]. The backward loop is important so we don’t reuse the same element multiple times in the same iteration.

At the end, return dp[target].

Edge cases I’d watch out for: handling empty arrays (sum is 0, so I’d return true), very small arrays (like size 1, which can never be partitioned unless it’s 0), and making sure the dp array index never goes out of bounds. In C++/Java, I’d also be careful about integer overflow when summing, so I might use a 64-bit type for the total before deciding on target.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you covered the key implementation details well. As a final question on this topic: how would you extend your approach if, instead of just deciding whether a partition is possible, you had to return one actual subset that achieves the target sum (or both subsets), and what extra space or bookkeeping would you add to reconstruct the answer?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to reconstruct an actual subset, I’d add some parent/choice information to the DP.

One simple way is to switch back to a 2D DP: dp[i][s] = whether we can get sum s using the first i elements. While filling it, I’d remember transitions: if dp[i][s] is true because dp[i-1][s] is true, we “skipped” a[i-1]; if it’s true because dp[i-1][s - a[i-1]] is true, we “took” a[i-1]. After filling, if dp[n][target] is true, I’d walk backwards from (n, target), following these choices: whenever we “took” a[i-1], I’d add it to the subset and subtract its value from the current sum. That gives me one subset; the other subset is just the remaining elements.

Space-wise, that’s O(n * target) for the DP table plus either a parallel choice table or you can infer choices directly from dp[i][s] vs dp[i-1][s] / dp[i-1][s - a[i-1]].

topic: Rotate a 2D matrix by 90 degrees.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you rotate an n x n 2D matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place, without using extra matrix storage? Walk me through the core idea first, then the step-by-step algorithm you’d implement.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place, I’d use the transpose-then-reverse-rows trick.

First, transpose the matrix: for all i from 0 to n-1, and j from i+1 to n-1, swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]. That flips it over the main diagonal.

Then, for each row i, reverse that entire row in-place (two-pointer swap from left to right). After the transpose, reversing each row gives the 90-degree clockwise rotation without needing an extra matrix.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now, suppose you could not use the transpose-then-reverse trick and instead had to do the 90-degree clockwise rotation by moving elements in-place layer by layer (ring by ring). How would you describe that algorithm, and what are its time and space complexities?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for the layer-by-layer approach, I think of the matrix as concentric squares. For each layer `layer` from 0 to n/2 - 1, I set `first = layer` and `last = n - 1 - layer`. Then I iterate `i` from `first` to `last - 1`, and for each i I do a 4-way swap:

Save top = matrix[first][i].  
Move left to top: matrix[first][i] = matrix[last - (i - first)][first].  
Move bottom to left: matrix[last - (i - first)][first] = matrix[last][last - (i - first)].  
Move right to bottom: matrix[last][last - (i - first)] = matrix[i][last].  
Move saved top to right: matrix[i][last] = top.

That rotates one “ring” in-place. Time complexity is O(n^2) since we touch each element once, and space complexity is O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and the index math was correct. Now imagine the matrix is not guaranteed to be square (it can be n x m); how would you rotate it 90 degrees clockwise if you are allowed extra space, and what changes in your algorithm and complexity compared to the in-place n x n version?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so if the matrix is n x m and I want to rotate it 90 degrees clockwise with extra space, I’d still keep the same dimensions, n x m, and just remap indices.

Conceptually, I’d create a new matrix result[n][m]. For each cell (i, j) in the original, I’d place it at (j, n - 1 - i) in the result. That way, I’m just doing a single pass over all elements, so time is O(n * m) and space is also O(n * m), pretty similar to the square case but with the rectangular bounds.

topic: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree so that the original structure is fully preserved? Please walk me through what traversal you’d pick, how you’d represent nulls, and the exact string (or byte) format you’d use.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d use a preorder traversal with explicit null markers. For serialize, I’d do a DFS: for each node, append its value to a list, and when I hit a null child, append a special token like "#" instead. Join the list with commas to get a string, e.g. "1,2,#,#,3,#,#".

For deserialize, I’d split the string by commas into a queue or use an index, then recursively rebuild: read the next token; if it’s "#", return null; otherwise create a node with that value, then recursively build its left and right subtrees in that order. Because preorder plus explicit nulls uniquely defines the tree structure, this fully preserves the original tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now suppose the tree is extremely large and might not fit fully in memory; how would you adapt your serialize/deserialize approach to work in a streaming fashion, and what trade-offs would you consider compared to your original recursive solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so for streaming I’d avoid recursion and materializing the whole string. For serialize, I’d do an iterative preorder with an explicit stack, writing each value or “#” directly to an OutputStream as I visit it, so memory stays O(tree height). For deserialize, I’d read tokens from an InputStream one by one and reconstruct iteratively (or with a shallow recursion) using a stack that tracks whether we’re filling a left or right child next. The main trade-offs are: code is more complex, you lose random access to the serialized data, and you rely on a stable streaming source, but you gain much better memory behavior for huge trees.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and thoughtful. Now imagine this is a complete binary tree with millions of nodes; can you propose a more space-efficient serialization than storing explicit null markers, and explain how you’d deserialize from that compact representation?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: For a complete binary tree I don’t need null markers because the shape is implied. I can store nodes in an array in level-order (heap style): the root at index 0, for a node at i its children are at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and I just store N (the node count) plus the N values in order. To deserialize, I read N, create an array of N nodes, fill their values, then for each i set left = node[2i+1] and right = node[2i+2] when those indices are < N; node[0] is the root.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on for complete trees. Now, suppose the tree is an arbitrary binary tree but you want a more compact representation than explicit “#” nulls; can you describe a scheme that encodes just the tree shape separately from the node values (for example as a bitstring), and explain how you’d decode it back into the original tree?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:

To decode, I walk the bitstring and the value array together with an index into each. When I see a 0 bit, I return null. When I see a 1 bit, I create a node using the next value from the values array, then recursively build its left and right children by consuming the next bits. topic: Find the first missing positive integer in an unsorted array.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the first missing positive integer in an unsorted array in O(n) time and O(1) extra space? Please walk me through the core idea before going into edge cases.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the key idea is to use the array itself as a hash to place each positive integer in its "correct" index. For an array of length n, the only relevant values are in the range [1, n], because anything ≤ 0 or > n can't be the first missing positive.

I iterate through the array, and while the current number x is in [1, n] and not already in its correct spot, I swap it into index x - 1. I keep doing this until every value that can be placed correctly is at position value - 1. After that, I scan the array once: the first index i where nums[i] != i + 1 means i + 1 is the first missing positive. If all positions are correct, then the answer is n + 1. This runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you hit the in-place hashing idea well. Now, suppose the array is extremely large and stored on disk (you can only stream through it a few times and don’t have random access); how would you adapt your approach to still find the first missing positive, and what trade-offs would you consider in terms of passes over the data and memory usage?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d basically do the same thing but in a streaming way. Since I can’t do random access, I’d keep a single pass over the data and maintain a running “current smallest missing positive” variable.

As I stream, every time I see a number equal to that current smallest missing, I just increment it by one. If I see numbers bigger than that, I ignore them, and if I see smaller ones, I’ve already accounted for them. After one pass, whatever value that variable holds is the first missing positive. This way I only need O(1) memory and a single pass, so it scales fine even if the array is on disk.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear but incorrect, because in a single streaming pass you can’t reliably know that all smaller positives have appeared. conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so negatives and numbers larger than n just naturally get ignored by the swapping condition, and duplicates are handled by checking if the target position already has the same value before swapping.

For [3, 4, -1, 1], n = 4.

Start i = 0, nums = [3, 4, -1, 1]. nums[0] = 3, in [1,4], target index 2 has -1, so swap -> [ -1, 4, 3, 1 ].
Still i = 0, nums[0] = -1, out of range, move on.

i = 1, nums[1] = 4, target index 3 has 1, swap -> [ -1, 1, 3, 4 ].
Still i = 1, nums[1] = 1, target index 0 has -1, swap -> [ 1, -1, 3, 4 ].
Still i = 1, nums[1] = -1, out of range, move on.

i = 2, nums[2] = 3, already at correct spot (index 2 = 3 - 1), move on.
i = 3, nums[3] = 4, also correct.

Now scan: index 0 has 1 (correct), index 1 has -1 (not 2), so the first missing positive is 2.

topic: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a BST.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the lowest common ancestor of two given nodes in a Binary Search Tree, assuming all node values are unique? First, describe the intuition using the BST property, then outline both a recursive and an iterative solution and their time/space complexities.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so in a BST, for any node, all values in the left subtree are smaller and all in the right subtree are larger. For two nodes p and q, their LCA is the first node where the paths to p and q diverge.

Intuition: Starting from the root, if both p and q have values smaller than the current node, you know the LCA must be in the left subtree. If both are greater, it must be in the right subtree. If one is smaller and the other greater (or one equals the current node), then the current node is the LCA.

Recursive solution:
If root is null, return null.
If p.val < root.val and q.val < root.val, recurse on root.left.
Else if p.val > root.val and q.val > root.val, recurse on root.right.
Else return root (this is the split point, so it’s the LCA).

Iterative solution:
Use a loop starting at root:
While current is not null:
- If p.val and q.val are both less than current.val, move current = current.left.
- Else if both are greater, move current = current.right.
- Else return current.

Time complexity for both is O(h), where h is the height of the tree, since we only traverse down one path. Space complexity is O(h) for the recursive version due to the call stack, and O(1) for the iterative version.

conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the tree is no longer a BST but a general binary tree (no ordering property). This would still give me O(h) time where h is the height of the tree, and O(1) space if I implement it iteratively.

topic: Find subset sum equal to target.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you approach the subset-sum problem: given an array of positive integers and a target T, determine if there exists a subset whose sum is exactly T? First, walk me through a straightforward brute-force solution and then describe how you’d improve it using dynamic programming, including the time and space complexities of both.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the brute-force way is to consider every subset and check if any sums to T. You can do this with recursion or bitmasking: for each element, either include it or not, leading to 2^n subsets and O(2^n) time, with O(n) stack space if recursive.

To improve it with dynamic programming, since the numbers and target are positive, we can use a boolean DP table where dp[i][s] means: using the first i elements, can we make sum s? The transition is: dp[i][s] = dp[i-1][s] || (s >= a[i-1] && dp[i-1][s - a[i-1]]). Initialize dp[0][0] = true and the answer is dp[n][T]. This runs in O(n*T) time and O(n*T) space. We can optimize space to O(T) by keeping only one dimension and iterating sums backwards for each element.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now, suppose instead of just deciding if a subset with sum T exists, you need to actually return one such subset if it exists; how would you modify your DP solution to reconstruct the subset, and what would the reconstruction step’s time and space overhead look like?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so you’re asking how to adjust the DP to count how many subsets sum to T, not just decide existence.

So instead of a boolean dp, I’d use an integer dp array where dp[s] is the number of ways to form sum s. The transition would be something like: for each value a[i], iterate s from T down to a[i] and do dp[s] += dp[s - a[i]]. Initialize dp[0] = 1 (empty subset) and everything else 0. In the end, dp[T] tells you how many subsets reach sum T.

Time stays O(n*T) and space is O(T). The overhead compared to the boolean version is basically just using integers and doing additions instead of ORs.

conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I want to reconstruct all possible subsets, not just one, I’d basically treat the DP table as a graph and do a DFS over it.

Starting from dp[n][T], whenever a state is reachable from either “take” or “not take”, I’d branch both ways: if dp[i-1][s] is true, I recurse without including a[i-1]; if s ≥ a[i-1] and dp[i-1][s - a[i-1]] is true, I recurse including a[i-1] and move to (i-1, s - a[i-1]). I’d carry along a temporary vector representing the current subset, and whenever I reach s = 0, I add that subset to the results.

Time in the worst case can blow up to proportional to the number of valid subsets times n, but the DP table itself is still O(n*T). The extra overhead is mainly storing all those subsets, which in the worst case is large, but asymptotically the DP/backtracking infrastructure is O(n*T) space and the traversal is bounded by the number of solutions times the depth n.

topic: Search a 2D matrix for a target value.

For a mid index, I map it back to 2D as: row = mid / n and col = mid % n, then compare matrix[row][col] with the target and adjust the search range accordingly. That gives time complexity O(log(m*n)), which is O(log m + log n), and space complexity O(1) since I’m only using a few variables.

Because rows and columns are both sorted, any element to the “left” in this flattened view is guaranteed to be smaller and any to the “right” is larger, so binary search is valid. That would give me time complexity O(log(m*n)) and space O(1).

topic: Given stock prices, compute max profit with unlimited transactions.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you’re given an array of stock prices where prices[i] is the price on day i, and you can buy and sell as many times as you like (but you must sell before you buy again). How would you compute the maximum profit, and what time and space complexities does your approach achieve?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so if I’m allowed to buy and sell multiple times, but I’m only allowed to hold at most one share at a time, I’d probably use a dynamic programming approach similar to the single-transaction problem.

I’d track two states for each day: one for the minimum price seen so far and one for the maximum profit so far, and update them as I go. For each price, I’d compute the potential profit if I sold on that day based on the global minimum, and update the max profit accordingly. Since I’m always reusing just those two variables, the time complexity would be O(n) and the space complexity would be O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your approach is clear but it’s actually solving the single-transaction problem; here you’re allowed unlimited transactions, as long as you don’t hold more than one share at a time. Given that, can you walk me through how you’d modify your logic or states so that multiple buy-sell pairs are captured correctly, maybe with a small example like [1, 2, 3, 1, 5]?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for unlimited transactions the greedy idea works: you just take every increasing segment. 

For the example [1, 2, 3, 1, 5], I’d accumulate profit whenever prices[i] > prices[i-1]. So profit = (2-1) + (3-2) + (5-1) = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6. Implementationally, I’d loop from i = 1 to n-1, and if prices[i] > prices[i-1], add prices[i] - prices[i-1] to the total. That’s O(n) time and O(1) space, and it’s equivalent to buying at local minima and selling at local maxima.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the right intuition with the greedy “sum of all positive deltas” view. Now, suppose there is a transaction fee f that you must pay on every sell operation; how would you modify your algorithm to maximize profit, and can you briefly justify why it’s still correct?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so with a transaction fee on every sell, the simple “sum all positive deltas” breaks, and it’s easier to think in terms of DP states.

I’d track two values as I scan prices:  
cash = max profit when I’m not holding a stock, hold = max profit when I am holding a stock.

Transitions for each price p are:
newCash = max(cash, hold + p - fee)        // either do nothing, or sell today and pay fee  
newHold = max(hold, cash - p)              // either keep holding, or buy today

Then set cash = newCash, hold = newHold.  
Answer is cash at the end. This is O(n) time, O(1) space, and the fee is baked into each sell action via the transition.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Nice, that DP with cash/hold states is spot on and your reasoning is clear. Let’s do one last twist: suppose now you still have unlimited transactions but you must wait at least one day after selling before buying again (a 1-day cooldown). How would you adapt your state definitions and transitions to handle this cooldown constraint?

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speech:

Or are you okay if I conceptually have those three but maybe collapse some of them into two variables if the transitions allow it?

topic: Find the minimum number of jumps to reach the end of an array.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Given an array where each element represents the maximum jump length from that position, how would you compute the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index, and can you explain both a greedy approach and why a simple DP might be suboptimal in practice?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: are we assuming that it’s always possible to reach the last index from the first one, or do I also need to handle cases where the end is unreachable and return something special? And when you say “simple DP might be suboptimal,” do you mean in terms of time complexity, space, or both?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions; I’ll treat your understanding as clear. Assume it is always possible to reach the last index, and when I say DP is suboptimal I mainly mean in terms of time complexity for large inputs, with some space overhead as well. Now, under those assumptions, how would you design a greedy O(n) algorithm to compute the minimum jumps, and what key invariants would you maintain as you scan the array?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d do it like this: I’d scan the array and at each index just pick the next index that has the largest value, because that means from there I can jump the farthest. So greedily, every step I move to the position with the maximum nums[j] within my current jump range, and I increment the jump count.

The invariant I’d maintain is that I’m always standing on the index with the maximum jump value seen so far, so that guarantees I minimize the number of jumps, since I’m always picking the locally best “power” to jump from. This way it’s still O(n), because I just look at each element once and always move to the max-valued one next.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a confident attempt, but the strategy of jumping to the index with the largest value in range is actually wrong; for example, in [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] it would not give the optimal answer, so I’d classify your last answer as wrong. Let’s simplify: conceptually, how is this problem similar to doing a BFS over levels of reachable indices, and how could you simulate that “level by level” behavior in a single linear scan without an explicit queue?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so when you say “similar to BFS over levels,” do you mean that each jump corresponds to one BFS level, like all indices reachable with 1 jump, then 2 jumps, and so on? conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Yes, exactly, your understanding of the BFS analogy is clear. conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
