conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so using merge sort, we already split the array into two sorted halves: left and right. While merging, we use two pointers i and j. If left[i] <= right[j], we just copy left[i] and move i. If left[i] > right[j], that means right[j] forms an inversion with every remaining element in the left half, because left and right are individually sorted. So we add (mid - i + 1) to the inversion count, copy right[j], and move j. We do this recursively and sum the counts from the left half, right half, and the cross inversions in the merge step.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

Now, suppose the array elements are very large (say up to 10^9) and you’d like to count inversions using a Binary Indexed Tree or Segment Tree instead of merge sort — how would you adapt the approach, and why might you need coordinate compression here?

Since x can be as large as 10^9, I can’t use its raw value as an index. So I do coordinate compression: take all values, sort them, map each distinct value to a rank from 1..K, and then use that rank as the index in the BIT/Segment Tree. That keeps the structure size O(N) while still preserving order.

conversation.speech: Nice, that was clear and spot on with the BIT + compression idea. 2) countGreaterRight[j] = how many k > j with a[k] > a[j]

Then the number of triplets with middle j is countLessLeft[j] * countGreaterRight[j], and I sum that over all j.

To get those counts in O(N log N), I’d use coordinate compression and two BIT passes: one left-to-right to fill countLessLeft (query how many elements < a[j] seen so far, then update with a[j]), and one right-to-left to fill countGreaterRight (query how many elements > a[j] to the right, then update).

topic: Reorder a linked list: L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1…

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you reorder a singly linked list in-place from L0→L1→L2→…→Ln into L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1→L2→Ln−2→…? Walk me through the high-level approach, including how you’d handle finding the middle, reversing, and merging without using extra space like an array.

conversation.speaker: interviewee

First, find the middle of the list using slow and fast pointers. When fast reaches the end, slow will be at the middle. I’ll split the list into two halves at slow: first half starts at head, second half starts at slow->next, and I set slow->next to null.

Second, reverse the second half of the list iteratively (using three pointers: prev, curr, next).

Third, merge the two lists by alternating nodes: take one from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, relinking next pointers as I go, until the second half is exhausted. This gives the L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1… order without extra space.

conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the standard 3-step approach. Because of prev pointers, I don’t need to worry about breaking anything; the list will just naturally reorder as I relink next and prev in this loop. We have three phases: finding the middle with slow/fast, reversing the second half, and then merging. Each of those traverses a portion of the list at most once, so overall we touch each node a constant number of times, which guarantees O(n) time and the algorithm always finishes.

For very small lists like length 1, 2, or 3, the fast pointer either never moves much or hits null quickly, so the “second half” is either empty or a single node. Reversing an empty or single-node list is a no-op, and then the merge step does essentially nothing, so we don’t get stuck in any extra work. topic: Find minimum meeting rooms required given intervals.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you approach the problem of finding the minimum number of meeting rooms required, given a list of meeting intervals with start and end times? Please walk me through your high-level idea first, then mention the time and space complexity of your preferred solution.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so given intervals [start, end], I’d first sort them by start time. Then I’d use a min-heap that stores end times of meetings currently using rooms.

I iterate through the sorted intervals: for each meeting, I compare its start time with the smallest end time in the heap. If the start time is >= the smallest end time, I pop from the heap (reuse that room). Then I push the current meeting’s end time onto the heap. The size of the heap at any point is the number of rooms in use, and the maximum size observed is the minimum number of rooms required.

Time complexity: O(n log n) due to sorting and heap operations.  
Space complexity: O(n) in the worst case for the heap.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now, suppose you cannot use extra space beyond O(1) apart from sorting the intervals array itself; can you think of an approach (even if it’s a bit less clean) to compute the minimum number of rooms using only the sorted intervals, and explain its time and space complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so if I’m constrained to O(1) extra space, I’d drop the heap and use the fact that we only need counts, not actual room assignments.

One standard way is: extract all start times and end times into two arrays, sort both, then use two pointers to sweep and track how many meetings are currently active. But if I truly cannot use extra arrays beyond the given one, I can’t do that cleanly without mutating the input in a tricky way.

So under a strict O(1) extra space constraint with only the original intervals array, I’d say there isn’t a clean, general solution that beats the heap approach asymptotically. Anything simulating it with in-place tricks tends to devolve into O(n²) scans to count overlaps, which is O(1) space but too slow. So: O(1) space is possible with a naive overlap-counting algorithm, but it’s O(n²) time; the optimal O(n log n) time solution realistically needs O(n) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your reasoning is clear. Let’s switch gears slightly: suppose meetings can be added and canceled online (a stream of add-interval and remove-interval operations), and at any time you need to answer “what is the current minimum number of rooms needed?” How would you design a data structure or system API to support this efficiently, and what would the complexities of each operation be?

conversation.speaker: interviewee

One approach is an ordered map (like a balanced BST) of time → delta, where adding a meeting [s, e) does `+1` at s and `-1` at e, and removing does the opposite. If the map also stores, in each node, the prefix-sum max for its subtree (like an order-statistics/augmented BST), then the current minimum rooms is just the global maximum prefix sum at the root. 

Each add/remove is O(log n) to update two keys and fix augmented data on the path; query for “current rooms needed” is O(1) from the root.

topic: Find the longest substring without repeating characters.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters in a given string, and what time and space complexity would your approach have? Please talk through the core idea before diving into details.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d use a sliding window with two pointers and a hash map (or array) to track the last seen index of each character.

I’d move the right pointer over the string, and for each character, if it’s already in the map and its last seen index is within the current window, I move the left pointer to one past that index. Then I update the character’s last seen index and compute the current window length as right - left + 1, keeping track of the maximum.

Time complexity is O(n), since each character is visited at most twice (entering and leaving the window), and space complexity is O(min(n, k)), where k is the character set size (often just O(k) like 26 or 128/256).

topic: Given an array of integers and a target, return indices of two numbers that add up to the target.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: For the two-sum problem, walk me through a brute-force solution first, then an optimized solution using a hash map: explain both the time and space complexities, and why the hash map changes the complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for the brute-force solution, I’d use two nested loops: for each index i, scan all j > i and check if nums[i] + nums[j] == target. If it matches, return [i, j]. That’s O(n²) time because of the double loop, and O(1) extra space.

For the optimized version, I’d use a hash map from value to index. I iterate once through the array, and for each nums[i], I compute complement = target - nums[i]. If the complement is already in the map, I return [map[complement], i]. Otherwise, I store nums[i] → i in the map and continue. This runs in O(n) time on average because each lookup/insert in the hash map is O(1), and it uses O(n) extra space for the map. The hash map changes the complexity by trading extra memory for constant-time lookups, avoiding the nested loop.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot-on. Now, suppose the input array is sorted in non-decreasing order and you need to solve the same two-sum problem but you are not allowed to use extra space beyond O(1). How would you approach it, and what are the time and space complexities?

conversation.speech: Right, so if the array is already sorted and I need O(1) extra space, I’d use a two-pointer approach. I put one pointer at the start (left = 0) and one at the end (right = n - 1). While left < right, I compute sum = nums[left] + nums[right]. If sum == target, I return those indices. If sum < target, I move left++ to increase the sum; if sum > target, I move right-- to decrease it. This runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Clear and correct. Now imagine the array is not sorted and may contain negative numbers, but you are not allowed to use extra space beyond O(1), and you still want better than O(n²) if possible — would you consider sorting the array to apply two pointers, and how would you handle the fact that sorting loses the original indices (walk me through your reasoning and trade-offs)?

conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I’m restricted to O(1) extra space and want better than O(n²), I’d consider in-place sorting like heapsort or an in-place quicksort variant. That gives me O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space, and then I can use the two-pointer approach.

But the catch is indices. If I sort just the values, I lose the mapping to original indices. Normally I’d store pairs (value, index) and sort by value, but that’s O(n) extra space, which violates the constraint. Without that, I can return the values that sum to target, but not the original positions. So there’s a trade-off: either respect O(1) space and return only values with O(n log n) time, or use O(n) space (value, index pairs or a hash map) to return original indices in O(n) or O(n log n) time. Under a strict “return indices + O(1) space” requirement, I don’t see a way to beat O(n²).

topic: Merge two sorted linked lists.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you merge two already sorted singly linked lists into a single sorted list in-place, and what edge cases would you watch out for in your implementation?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so I’d use two pointers, one for each list, say p1 and p2. I’d also keep a dummy head and a tail pointer that always points to the end of the merged list. Then I’d iterate while both p1 and p2 are non-null, compare their values, attach the smaller node to tail->next, advance that list’s pointer, and move tail forward. Once one list is exhausted, I just attach the remaining part of the other list to tail->next. That way it’s all done in-place by relinking next pointers, no new nodes created.

Edge cases I’d watch for are: one or both input lists being null, all nodes coming from just one list because it’s always smaller, and making sure I don’t lose track of next pointers when relinking (so I’d store next before moving the pointer if needed).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear; you described the standard iterative solution well. Now suppose these two sorted linked lists are extremely long and you have very limited call stack, but for some reason you’re asked to implement the merge recursively instead of iteratively—how would the recursive approach work, and what trade-offs or risks would you call out compared to the iterative version?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot-on for the recursive trade-offs. Now imagine you’re given k sorted linked lists instead of just two; how would you extend your approach to efficiently merge all k lists into one sorted list, and what time complexity would your preferred solution achieve in terms of total number of nodes N and k?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for k lists I’d avoid pairwise merging one by one because that can get expensive. I’d use a min-heap (priority queue) of size k, where each entry is the current head node of a list keyed by its value. 

I push all non-null heads into the heap, then repeatedly pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and if that node has a next, push its next back into the heap. This touches each of the N total nodes once, and each heap operation is O(log k), so overall time is O(N log k), with O(k) extra space for the heap.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you picked the optimal heap-based approach. Let’s shift slightly: suppose instead of linked lists, you have two sorted arrays in memory, and enough extra space at the end of the first array to hold all elements; how would you merge them in-place without using extra arrays, and why is it better to go from the end rather than from the beginning?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d use three indices: i at the end of the valid part of the first array, j at the end of the second array, and k at the very end of the first array’s total capacity. Then I compare from the back: while i and j are in range, place the larger of A[i] and B[j] at A[k], and move that pointer and k left. If one array is exhausted, copy the remaining elements of the other (usually just from B) into A.

Going from the end is important because it avoids overwriting unprocessed elements in the first array. If I started from the beginning and wrote into A, I could destroy values I haven’t compared yet.

topic: Solve Sudoku using backtracking.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Walk me through how you would represent the Sudoku board and the helper checks (row/column/subgrid validity) in code before you even start backtracking; what data structures would you choose and why?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d represent the Sudoku board as a 9x9 array (or vector) of integers, where 0 represents an empty cell. For the helper checks, the simplest is to scan the row, column, and 3x3 box each time and see if the number already exists.

If I want it a bit more efficient, I’d keep three 9x9 boolean arrays: row[9][10], col[9][10], box[9][10], where row[r][num] is true if num is already used in row r, similarly for columns and boxes (with box index = (r/3)*3 + c/3). That way, checking validity is just O(1) lookups rather than scanning every time.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear. Now, describe the recursive backtracking strategy itself: how do you choose the next cell to fill, how do you try candidates, and how do you unwind the state (including your row/col/box structures) when backtracking?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d write a recursive function that tries to fill the board cell by cell. The simplest is to scan from top-left to bottom-right to find the next empty cell (value 0). For that cell, I iterate num from 1 to 9, and for each num I check row/col/box validity using the boolean arrays; if it’s valid, I place num in the board, mark row/col/box as used, and recurse to fill the next empty cell.

If the recursive call returns true, I propagate true up (solution found). If it returns false, I backtrack: reset the board cell to 0, and clear the corresponding row/col/box flags, then try the next num. If no num works for that cell, I return false to force more backtracking.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear. Now suppose the Sudoku has multiple valid solutions: how would you modify your backtracking function to either stop at the first solution or enumerate all solutions, and what impact does that have on time complexity in the worst case?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so by default my function returns a bool and stops at the first solution: as soon as a recursive call returns true, I just bubble that up and don’t explore further branches.

To enumerate all solutions, I’d change the behavior so that instead of returning immediately on success, I record the current board (e.g., push it into a vector of boards) and then continue backtracking to look for more, ultimately returning when the whole search space is explored. In the worst case, enumerating all solutions means exploring essentially the full backtracking tree, which is exponential in the number of empty cells; stopping at the first solution can prune a lot earlier, but the theoretical worst-case time is still exponential.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear. Now, how would you make your solver significantly faster on hard puzzles: describe at least one heuristic for choosing the next cell or pruning candidates (e.g., MRV / most constrained variable), and explain how you’d integrate it into your current design and what trade-offs it introduces.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so one common heuristic is MRV: always pick the empty cell with the fewest valid candidates. Instead of scanning for the first 0, I’d scan the whole board, and for each empty cell quickly count how many numbers 1–9 are allowed using my row/col/box structures, then choose the cell with the smallest count.

This adds an O(81 * 9) scan per recursive step, but in practice it prunes the search tree a lot because we hit dead-ends earlier on the most constrained cells. For even more speed, I could maintain a tiny array of candidate counts per cell and update it incrementally when I place/remove a number, but that makes the code more complex and bookkeeping heavier.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear. Let’s shift perspective: how would you prove or argue that your backtracking solver is correct (i.e., it finds a solution iff one exists and the solution respects all Sudoku rules), and what invariants does your recursion maintain throughout the search?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify what you’re looking for. Do you want a more formal, almost proof-style argument about correctness and termination of the recursive algorithm, or more of an informal explanation of why the recursion plus the validity checks guarantees we don’t miss any solutions or accept invalid ones? Also, when you say “invariants,” are you thinking about conditions on the board and the helper structures that must hold at every recursive call?

topic: Given an array, find all unique triplets that sum to zero.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you solve the “3-sum” problem: given an integer array, return all unique triplets (i, j, k) such that nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] = 0? Talk through a brute-force approach first, then walk me to an optimized solution, including how you’d avoid duplicate triplets and what the time and space complexities are.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so brute force first: I could try all triplets with three nested loops (i < j < k) and check if nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. To avoid duplicates there, I’d probably put each valid triplet into a set (like storing a sorted tuple) and convert back to a list at the end. That’s O(n³) time and at least O(m) extra space for m triplets, plus any set overhead.

For an optimized solution, I’d sort the array first. Then I’d fix one index i from 0 to n-3, and for each i, use a two-pointer approach on the subarray (i+1 … n-1): left = i+1, right = n-1. Compute sum = nums[i] + nums[left] + nums[right]. If sum < 0, move left++; if sum > 0, move right--; if it’s 0, record that triplet, then move both pointers while skipping over duplicates (increment left while nums[left] is the same as previous, similarly decrement right). To avoid duplicate triplets from the first element, I’d also skip nums[i] if it’s the same as nums[i-1]. That gives O(n²) time due to the outer loop plus two-pointer scan, and O(1) extra space aside from the output.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on for the classic 3-sum. Now, suppose the array is extremely large and stored on disk (you can’t load it all into memory), but you still need all unique triplets summing to zero; how would you adapt your approach in an external-memory / streaming setting, and what trade-offs would you consider in terms of I/O, time, and memory?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify the setup. When you say the array is extremely large and on disk, do you mean I can still make multiple passes over the data and use external sorting / chunking, or are you thinking of more of a single-pass streaming model where I only see each element once or in small windows? Also, is an approximate solution acceptable, or do you specifically want all exact unique triplets?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarification question; let’s say you’re allowed multiple passes over the data and can do external sorting, but main memory is much smaller than the array, and you must still find all exact unique triplets. How would you adapt your 3-sum algorithm to this external-memory setting, and what would be the main bottlenecks and optimizations you’d think about?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d treat this mostly as a distributed problem rather than an external-memory one. I’m thinking: first I’d partition the array across multiple machines, have each machine load its chunk into memory, sort it locally, and then run the usual O(n²) 3-sum with two pointers within that chunk. Each worker would emit the triplets it finds, and then we’d have a final aggregation step that deduplicates triplets across machines, maybe by sorting the triplets themselves or using a distributed hash.

The main bottleneck would be the network shuffle and dedup phase, since you might generate overlapping triplets across partitions, and also the cost of sorting on each worker. To optimize, I’d try to balance partitions so that each machine handles roughly equal work and maybe compress or encode the triplets efficiently before sending them to the reducer for deduplication.

topic: Given intervals, merge all overlapping intervals.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: We’ve picked the topic “merge overlapping intervals” — can you walk me through the algorithm you’d use, including how you’d handle sorting, the merge logic, and the final time and space complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay so given a list of intervals like [start, end], I’d first sort them by their start value in ascending order. Then I’d iterate through the sorted list, maintaining a current interval (say `currStart`, `currEnd`). For each next interval `[s, e]`, if `s` is less than or equal to `currEnd`, they overlap, so I update `currEnd` to `max(currEnd, e)`. If `s` is greater than `currEnd`, there’s no overlap, so I push `[currStart, currEnd]` into the result and reset `currStart = s`, `currEnd = e`. After the loop, I add the last current interval to the result. Sorting takes O(n log n), the merge pass is O(n), so overall time is O(n log n), and space is O(n) for the output (or O(1) extra if we’re allowed to modify in place aside from the result).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That explanation was clear and correct. Now suppose your intervals are coming as an online stream (one interval at a time, potentially unbounded), and at any point you should be able to output the current merged set of intervals; how would you maintain and update the merged structure efficiently as new intervals arrive, and what data structures and complexities would you aim for?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, let me just clarify the requirements. When you say “online stream” and I should be able to output the current merged set at any point, do you mean:

1) I only need to support inserts of new intervals and occasional full reads of the merged set, or  
2) I also need to support queries like “which intervals overlap this point/range” in between?

Also, is it okay if the per-insert cost is something like O(log n) amortized, or are you aiming for something stricter?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions — let’s go with (1): you only need to support inserts of new intervals and occasional full reads of the merged, non-overlapping set; no point/range queries. Assume O(log n) amortized per insert is fine. Given that, describe a concrete data structure and how you’d handle insertion and merging as intervals arrive.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Okay, got it’s inserts plus occasional full reads. I just want to pin down one more thing: when you say “concrete data structure,” are you expecting me to stick to something from the standard library like a balanced BST keyed by start (e.g., map in C++ / TreeMap in Java), or are you looking for something more custom like an interval tree or segment tree? Also, is it acceptable if producing the full merged list takes O(k) where k is the number of merged intervals at that moment?

topic: Implement Bellman-Ford algorithm.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you implement the Bellman-Ford algorithm for a directed weighted graph: what data structures would you use, how would you detect a negative cycle, and what is the time and space complexity of your approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: do you want me to walk through a language-agnostic design of Bellman-Ford with the data structures and complexity, or actually describe it as if I were implementing it in a specific language like C++ or Java? Also, should I focus only on shortest-path from a single source, or also talk about reconstructing the actual paths?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question — let's keep it language-agnostic, but you can assume a typical imperative language like C++/Java, and focus on single-source shortest paths including how you would reconstruct the path. Can you now walk me through Bellman-Ford step by step, including initialization, the relaxation process, and negative-cycle detection?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so Bellman-Ford is a single-source shortest path algorithm that works even with negative edge weights, as long as there’s no negative cycle reachable from the source.

We keep a distance array dist[] of size V, initialized to +∞ for all vertices except the source, which is 0. To reconstruct paths, we also keep a parent[] (or predecessor) array, initialized to something like -1 or null.

We represent the graph as a list of edges (u, v, w). Then we run V-1 iterations. In each iteration, we go through every edge (u, v, w); if dist[u] + w < dist[v], we update dist[v] and set parent[v] = u. Repeating this V-1 times guarantees shortest paths if there’s no negative cycle.

To detect a negative cycle, we do one more pass over all edges. If we can still relax any edge (i.e., dist[u] + w < dist[v] is true for some edge), then there is a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.

To reconstruct the path to a target t, we follow parent[t] backward (t, parent[t], parent[parent[t]], …) until we reach the source or -1, and then reverse that sequence.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and complete. Now, can you analyze the time and space complexity of your Bellman-Ford implementation in terms of V and E, and briefly compare when you would choose Bellman-Ford over Dijkstra in practice?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Let me think… so with the edge-list implementation I described, we do V-1 iterations over all E edges, plus one more for negative-cycle detection. So the time complexity is O(V·E). Space-wise, we store the edge list O(E), plus dist[] and parent[] arrays O(V), so total space is O(V + E).

I’d choose Bellman-Ford when the graph can have negative edge weights and I still need shortest paths, or when I need explicit negative-cycle detection. Dijkstra is preferable when all edge weights are non-negative, because with a good priority queue it’s faster, O(E log V), on sparse graphs.

topic: Convert a sorted array into a balanced BST.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you convert a sorted array into a height-balanced BST, and what traversal order naturally prints the BST back into the same sorted array? Please walk through the core idea and its time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so, the key idea is to use the middle element of the sorted array as the root, because that balances the number of elements on the left and right. Recursively, you take the left half of the array to build the left subtree and the right half to build the right subtree.  

This is essentially a divide-and-conquer algorithm. The time complexity is O(n) because each element is visited once to create a node, and the extra space complexity is O(log n) for the recursion stack in a balanced tree.  

If you then perform an in-order traversal (left, root, right) on this BST, you naturally get back the elements in the same sorted order as the original array.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now, suppose the sorted array is extremely large and stored on disk (you can only read it sequentially once, like a stream) and you don’t know its length in advance; how would you build a height-balanced BST in that setting, and what trade-offs or approximations might you consider?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so in the pure streaming model where I only get one sequential pass and don’t know the length up front, I can’t do the classic “pick middle by index” approach exactly, because that needs random access or at least two passes.

One practical approach is to relax to “approximately balanced.” As I stream, I can insert into a self-balancing BST (like an AVL or Red-Black tree). Each insert is O(log n), so overall it’s O(n log n) time, O(n) space, but the resulting tree is height-balanced by the data structure itself.

If I really want the optimal O(n) construction, I’d need either: a first pass to count elements (so, two passes over the data), or to buffer everything into an array in memory or on disk and then do the normal middle-split recursion. The trade-off is between strict optimality (needs extra passes or storage) and a one-pass streaming solution with higher time complexity but acceptable balance using a self-balancing BST.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you correctly called out the trade-offs. Now imagine the sorted array is not unique and can contain many duplicates: how would you adapt your “sorted array to balanced BST” construction, and what are the implications for the tree’s shape and search complexity when handling duplicates (e.g., all equal elements)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me clarify one thing. Are you mostly asking about how to define the insertion/placement rule for duplicates during the construction (like always putting them on one side or grouping them), or are you asking whether I can change the data structure itself, for example by storing counts or lists at each node instead of one value per node?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question – think in the standard BST model where each node holds a single key, and duplicates must still respect the BST ordering (you can choose a consistent side for them). Given that, how would you modify your construction from a sorted array to a balanced BST to handle duplicates, and what happens to the tree shape and search complexity in extreme cases like when all elements are equal?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so given a sorted array with duplicates, the construction algorithm itself doesn’t really change: I still pick the middle index as the root, then recursively build left from the left half and right from the right half. Because the array is sorted, all elements in the left subarray are ≤ arr[mid], and in the right subarray are ≥ arr[mid]. I just need to pick a convention, like “duplicates go to the right,” and ensure my comparison in any later insert/search respects that.

In terms of shape: as long as I keep splitting by index mid, the tree remains height-balanced even if there are many duplicates, because balance depends on positions, not values. In the extreme case where all elements are equal, I still get a perfectly balanced tree (complete/near-complete), so search is still O(log n); I just may have to walk left/right according to my duplicate rule, but the height bound doesn’t change.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the right way to think about duplicates and shape. Last question: if I give you a height-balanced BST, how would you efficiently produce a sorted array from it, and then use that array to reconstruct a (potentially different) balanced BST with minimal extra space beyond the output array and the new tree nodes?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so, first I’d do an in-order traversal of the given BST to dump its values into a sorted array. That’s O(n) time and O(h) extra space for the recursion stack (or I could do Morris traversal to get O(1) extra, but recursion is usually fine).

Then, to reconstruct a balanced BST, I use the standard array-to-BST routine: recursively pick the middle element of the current subarray as the root, build the left subtree from the left half, and the right subtree from the right half. That also runs in O(n) time and only uses O(log n) extra stack space, with the array itself being the main storage.

topic: Perform level-order traversal of a binary tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you perform a level-order traversal of a binary tree? First describe the idea at a high level, then walk me through the data structures you’d use and the time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I’ll focus on how to construct the data structure for level-order traversal rather than just the traversal itself.

So I’d first store the tree nodes level by level in something like an array or list, where index 0 is the root, then its children, and so on. Essentially like how a heap is stored: for a node at index i, its left child is at 2i + 1 and right child at 2i + 2. That way, doing a level-order traversal is basically just iterating linearly over that array from start to end.

In terms of data structures, I’d use a dynamic array (like a vector) to hold the nodes in their level-order positions. Time complexity to build that structure from a pointer-based tree would be O(n), since I’d visit each node once, and then traversal is also O(n) because it’s just a single pass over the array. Space complexity is O(n) for storing all the nodes in the array.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a clear explanation, but you slightly shifted to how a tree might be stored in an array; I was asking more about traversing a regular pointer-based binary tree. Can you now describe how you’d perform level-order traversal using a queue on a standard binary tree node structure (with left/right pointers), and how you’d modify it if you wanted the result grouped by levels (list of lists)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for a normal pointer-based binary tree, I’d use a queue to do level-order traversal.

I’d push the root into the queue. Then while the queue isn’t empty, I pop the front node, visit it (e.g., print or collect its value), and push its left and right children if they’re not null. That visits nodes level by level. Time is O(n), space is O(n) in the worst case for the queue.

If I want the result grouped by levels (a list of lists), I’d add an outer loop: while the queue isn’t empty, I record the current queue size as levelSize, then run a for-loop levelSize times, popping nodes, adding their values into a temporary list for that level, and pushing their children. After that inner loop, I append the temporary list to the final result.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. As a follow-up, suppose the binary tree is so large it doesn’t fit into memory at once, but you have an iterator-like API that can stream nodes from disk in level order; how would you design an interface or approach to still expose a “level-order traversal” to a client, and what trade-offs would you consider around buffering and latency?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, let me make sure I understand the setup. When you say there’s an iterator-like API that can stream nodes from disk in level order, do you mean:

1) The underlying system already guarantees the nodes come out strictly in level-order, one by one, and I just need to wrap that in a nicer interface for clients?

Or 2) I still have to manage some notion of which children belong to which parent/level, possibly by doing my own buffering on top of a more primitive disk access API?

Also, are you imagining multiple passes over the data are allowed, or is it more of a single-pass streaming constraint?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions. Assume the underlying system already guarantees a single-pass, strict level-order stream of nodes (with enough metadata to know where levels start/end), and your job is to design an interface that lets clients either iterate node-by-node or consume one level at a time; how would you design that API and what buffering/latency and memory trade-offs would you consider?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, that makes sense. I’d probably expose two main methods on top of the underlying stream: something like `nextNode()` for node-by-node consumption, and `nextLevel()` that returns a list of nodes for the next level.

Internally, I’d have a small buffer tied to the current level. Since the underlying stream tells me where levels start and end, `nextLevel()` can keep pulling from the stream until the level boundary, store those nodes temporarily in a vector/list, return it, then discard the buffer. Memory usage is then proportional to the max width of a single level, not the whole tree.

For `nextNode()`, I can either: 1) just pass through directly to the underlying iterator for minimal buffering and lowest latency per node, or 2) reuse the same level buffer and just hand nodes out one by one from it. The main trade-off is: larger buffering (whole level) gives nicer batch interfaces but may increase latency before the first node of that level is delivered; minimal buffering keeps latency and memory low but gives the client more work if they want level grouping.

topic: Sliding window: find max in every window of size k.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you solve “find the maximum in every sliding window of size k over an array” in O(n) time, and why is a deque a good fit for this problem compared to using a heap or a balanced tree?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so the O(n) solution uses a deque that stores indices of elements in decreasing order of their values. As we move the window from left to right, for each index i we first pop from the back while the current element is greater than or equal to the elements at those indices, since they can never be maxima again. Then we push i to the back. We also pop from the front if the index at the front is now outside the current window (i - k + 1 > front). After the first k − 1 steps, the front of the deque always holds the index of the maximum for the current window.

A deque is ideal because we need fast insertions and deletions at both ends while maintaining this “monotonic” structure, and each element is added and removed at most once, giving O(n). A heap or balanced tree would give O(log k) per operation (for insert and delete), so overall O(n log k), and also makes it harder to lazily remove out-of-window elements without extra bookkeeping.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear. Now, suppose your array is a stream that is too large to fit entirely in memory, and you only see elements one by one while still needing the max of each window of size k in order. How, if at all, would you adapt your deque-based approach in a streaming context, and what constraints (memory, latency) could break this method?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so in a streaming context I’d actually need to store the whole window explicitly, because I have to know all k elements to decide the max. So I’d probably keep an array or list of the last k values, and then still use the deque logic on top of that.

As each new element arrives, I append it to this window array and, if the size exceeds k, I just drop the oldest one from both the array and the deque. This would mean I’m using O(k) memory for the window array plus O(k) for the deque, and that should still be fine even for large streams, since I’m not storing anything beyond the last k items.

If memory or latency becomes an issue, I guess the main problem would be if k itself is huge, because then I’d be holding too many elements; in that case, the deque approach might break down and I’d probably need something more approximate rather than exact maxima.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your earlier deque explanation was clear, but in the streaming follow-up you overcomplicated it a bit: you actually don’t need a separate array; the deque alone over indices (or timestamps) is enough to handle a stream. Let’s pivot slightly: how would you modify the sliding-window maximum algorithm if, instead of max, you needed the median in every window of size k, and what time complexity would you aim for and why?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so for sliding-window median you can’t really use the monotonic deque trick. A common approach is two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced so their sizes differ by at most one; the median is at the top. For the sliding window, on each step you insert the new element into one of the heaps, rebalance, and you also need to delete the element that’s leaving the window. Since standard heaps don’t support delete-in-O(log n) by value, you typically use “lazy deletion” with hash maps that track counts of elements to be removed. Each insert, delete, and rebalance is O(log k), so overall it’s O(n log k), which is acceptable and more or less optimal for exact medians with this data structure.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and on point. As a final twist on sliding windows: suppose you have an array of integers (can be negative) and a window size k, and you need the number of subarrays of length at most k whose sum is ≤ some threshold T; how would you approach this, and can you still use a classic sliding window, or what changes when negatives are allowed?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the key issue is the negatives. With all non‑negative numbers, a classic sliding window works because if you expand and the sum gets too big, shrinking from the left only decreases the sum, so the window boundaries move monotonically.

Once you allow negatives, that monotonicity breaks: shrinking from the left might actually increase the sum, so a two-pointer sliding window can skip valid subarrays or loop badly. For the “sum ≤ T, length ≤ k” version with negatives, I’d switch to prefix sums and some data structure over the last k prefixes. You look at prefix[i] and need to count j in [i−k, i−1] with prefix[i] − prefix[j] ≤ T, i.e. prefix[j] ≥ prefix[i] − T. So you can maintain the last k prefix sums in a balanced BST or Fenwick tree, support insert/erase as i moves, and for each i query how many are ≥ (prefix[i] − T). That’s O(n log k); you’re no longer in the simple O(n) sliding-window world once negatives are allowed.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear, especially the point about losing monotonicity with negatives. Let’s finish with a short conceptual one: when you see a problem, what mental checklist do you use to decide whether a sliding-window / two-pointer approach is applicable, and can you give a quick example where it looks tempting but is actually the wrong tool?  <END_OF_INTERVIEW>

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:

Also, do the constraints have some monotonic flavor, like “sum ≤ T” with non‑negative numbers, or “at most K distinct chars”, so that once a window is invalid, moving one pointer in a single direction will only move you towards validity.

A tempting but wrong case is “longest subarray with sum exactly K” when negatives are allowed. It sounds like classic sliding window, but because negatives break monotonicity of the sum, two pointers can’t safely shrink/expand without missing solutions; you need prefix sums and a hash map instead.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you’ve shown solid intuition around when sliding windows apply and when they break. We’ll wrap up here; thanks for walking through the variations in such a structured way.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I tie everything back to the original “max in every window of size k” problem, I’d say the main takeaway is picking the right data structure for the window state. For this specific problem, I’d still argue that a deque is the best fit because it gives you O(1) amortized updates while maintaining the candidates for the maximum in order.

If I tried to generalize that point too aggressively, like saying “just always use a deque for sliding windows,” that would be wrong. For example, when we moved to medians, the structure had to change to two heaps with lazy deletion, and for counting subarrays with constraints and negatives, we needed prefix sums plus a tree or Fenwick. So I’m reading your last comment as: the nuance is less about sliding window itself and more about recognizing which invariant and which data structure keep the per-step cost small.

topic: Find longest common prefix among a list of strings.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I’d do a vertical scan: take the first string as a reference and for each character position i from 0 to its length, compare s[0][i] with s[1][i], s[2][i], …, s[n-1][i]. As soon as I hit an index that’s out of bounds for some string or a mismatch, I stop and return the prefix up to i.

In the worst case, I compare up to L characters for each of the n strings, so the time complexity is O(n·L). I only use a few indices and maybe a result substring, so the extra space is O(1) (or O(L) if you count the output storage).

conversation.speech: That was clear and the complexity analysis is spot on. Now imagine the same problem, but the list of strings is extremely large and stored on disk, so reading all of them fully is expensive; can you think of an approach that minimizes disk I/O, and how its complexity compares to your previous solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d avoid loading all strings into memory at once and instead read them in a streaming, chunked way. One simple idea is to binary search on the prefix length L on disk: pick a candidate length mid, and for each string, just read the first mid characters and check if they’re all equal. If they are, move the lower bound up; if not, move it down. That way, for each string I only ever read up to the final prefix length (plus log L passes), rather than scanning character-by-character across the whole string set in memory. 

Asymptotically, this is O(n · L · log L) character reads in the worst case, which is a bit worse than O(n·L), but in practice it’s I/O-friendly because we do fewer small random reads and only touch a bounded prefix of each string, and we can batch reads in larger chunks.

Let’s shift slightly: how would you use a trie to compute the longest common prefix, what would its time and space complexity be, and in what scenarios (if any) would you prefer the trie-based approach over your simple vertical scan?

To get the LCP, I start at the root and walk down as long as the current node has exactly one child and is not the end of a word; the path I walk is the longest common prefix.

Building the trie takes O(total_chars) time, which is O(n·L), and space is also O(n·L) in the worst case for all the nodes. I’d prefer this approach when I’m going to reuse the trie for many prefix queries, autocomplete, or other operations – for a one-off LCP on a moderate list, the simple vertical scan is simpler and more space-efficient.

topic: Implement BFS and DFS traversal.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you implement BFS and DFS traversals on a graph represented with an adjacency list, and when would you prefer BFS over DFS in practice? Please walk through the traversal order you’d get on a small example graph of your choice.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so with an adjacency list, for BFS I’d use a queue and a visited set. Starting from a source node, I mark it visited, enqueue it, then repeatedly dequeue a node, process it, and enqueue all its unvisited neighbors, marking them visited as I go.

For DFS, I’d typically use recursion or an explicit stack. Starting from a source, I mark it visited, process it, then recursively (or via a stack) visit each unvisited neighbor, going as deep as possible before backtracking.

For example, say the graph is:
A: B, C
B: D
C: D
D: (none)

BFS from A gives: A, B, C, D.  
DFS from A (visiting neighbors in listed order) gives: A, B, D, C.

I’d prefer BFS when I need the shortest path in an unweighted graph or level-order information, like finding the minimum number of edges between two nodes. I’d prefer DFS when I care about exploring full paths, doing topological sort, or detecting cycles, especially when depth structure matters more than shortest distance.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Suppose your graph is large and stored on disk (so random access is expensive) and may even be disconnected; how would you adapt your BFS and DFS implementations to handle disconnected components and to be as memory- and IO-efficient as possible, and what tradeoffs would you make between the two traversals in this setting?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for disconnected graphs, I’d wrap the traversal in a loop over all nodes: for each node, if it’s not visited, start a BFS/DFS from there so every component gets covered.

For large, disk-backed graphs, I’d try to make access more sequential. For BFS, that might mean processing nodes level by level and batching neighbor fetches, maybe even storing adjacency lists clustered so a frontier expansion is mostly sequential reads. I’d also be careful with the visited structure, maybe a bitmap or Bloom filter to keep it memory-light.

DFS is more memory-efficient in terms of “frontier” size, but the access pattern is more random and can thrash the disk. So if IO is the bottleneck, I’d lean toward a more level-synchronous BFS with good layout even if it uses more RAM; if RAM is tighter and the graph fits reasonably in cacheable chunks, I’d consider DFS but might limit recursion depth or use an explicit stack plus some ordering to reduce random seeks.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your answer was clear and you’re thinking about the right tradeoffs. Staying with BFS/DFS, how would you modify these traversals to detect cycles in: (a) an undirected graph, and (b) a directed graph, and what’s the intuition behind why your methods work in each case?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so:

For an undirected graph, with DFS I’d track the parent of each node. When I see an edge to a visited neighbor that is not the parent, that’s a cycle. With BFS it’s similar: if I dequeue a node and see an already-visited neighbor that isn’t my parent, I’ve found a cycle. This works because in an undirected graph, the only “repeat” edge that’s allowed without a cycle is back to the node you came from.

For a directed graph, I’d use DFS with a 3-color or two-sets scheme: a “visited” set plus a “recursion stack” / “currently visiting” set. When I traverse, I mark a node as “in progress”; if I ever see an edge to a node that’s already “in progress”, that’s a back edge and indicates a cycle. Once I finish exploring a node, I mark it “done” / remove it from the recursion stack. This works because a back edge in the DFS tree means there’s a path from that node back to an ancestor, forming a directed cycle.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Last question on this topic: suppose your graph has up to 10^5 nodes and 10^6 edges in memory; how would you implement BFS and DFS iteratively to avoid stack overflows, and what are the time and space complexities for both traversals in terms of V and E, including the impact of using adjacency lists vs adjacency matrices?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for graphs that big I’d avoid recursion for DFS and use an explicit stack.

Iterative BFS: I’d use a queue (like std::queue), a visited array, and an adjacency list. Push the start node into the queue, mark visited, then while the queue isn’t empty, pop a node and push all its unvisited neighbors, marking them visited.

Iterative DFS: I’d use a stack (std::stack or vector used as a stack) plus a visited array. Push the start node, then while the stack isn’t empty, pop a node; if it’s not visited, mark it visited and push its neighbors onto the stack.

With adjacency lists, both BFS and DFS are O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space for the graph plus O(V) for visited and the queue/stack. With an adjacency matrix, time becomes O(V^2) because you scan all possible neighbors for each node, and space is O(V^2), which is much worse at this scale.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and fully correct. Let’s zoom out: how would you use BFS or DFS (or a combination) to solve each of these efficiently, and why: (a) finding all connected components, (b) checking if a directed graph is a DAG, and (c) finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph between two nodes when you only care about that single pair?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so:

a) For all connected components, I’d use BFS only. I’d start from an arbitrary node, run a single BFS, and that will always visit every node in the entire graph, so I get exactly one component that way and I’m done.

b) To check if a directed graph is a DAG, I’d just run a BFS from any node and if I don’t revisit any node, then there’s no cycle, so it must be a DAG. There’s no need for any special tracking beyond a single visited array.

c) For the shortest path in an unweighted graph between two nodes, I’d prefer DFS because it goes deep and finds a path quickly. The first path DFS finds between the source and target will always be the shortest one in terms of edge count, so I can stop as soon as I hit the target.

topic: Merge two sorted linked lists.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you merge two sorted singly linked lists into a single sorted list in-place, and what edge cases would you watch out for in your implementation?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d maintain two pointers, one for each input list, and build the merged list by always choosing the smaller current node.

First, I’d handle edge cases: if list1 is null, return list2; if list2 is null, return list1. Then I’d pick the smaller head as the start of the merged list and keep a tail pointer to the last node in the merged list. While both pointers are non-null, compare their values, attach the smaller node to tail->next, advance that list’s pointer, and move tail forward. At the end, one list might still have remaining nodes, so I’d attach the rest directly to tail->next.

Since I’m just relinking next pointers and not creating new nodes, it’s in-place and runs in O(m+n) time, O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct; your in-place approach and complexity analysis are solid. How would your merging logic change, if at all, if the lists were sorted in descending order, and can you briefly describe how you’d implement the same merge recursively and what trade-offs that introduces?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so if the lists are sorted in descending order, the core logic is the same but the comparison flips: instead of picking the smaller node each time, I’d pick the larger one (e.g., if l1->val > l2->val, attach l1, otherwise attach l2). Everything else about pointer movement and attaching the remainder stays the same.

Recursively, I’d define: if one list is null, return the other. Otherwise compare the current nodes, choose the one that should come first, set its next to the result of a recursive call on the remaining part of that list and the other list, and return that chosen node. The trade-off is cleaner, shorter code but O(m+n) stack space due to recursion depth, which risks stack overflow for very long lists, whereas the iterative version stays O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you called out the recursion trade-off well. Suppose you are given k sorted linked lists instead of just two; how would you efficiently merge all k into one sorted list, what time and space complexity would your approach have, and how would that compare to a naive pairwise merge strategy?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for k sorted lists, the efficient way is to use a min-heap (priority queue) of size k. I push the head of each non-empty list into the heap keyed by node value. Then I repeatedly pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and if that node has a next, push its next into the heap. This visits each of the N total nodes once, and each heap op costs O(log k), so overall time is O(N log k) and extra space is O(k) for the heap.

A naive strategy where you merge lists one by one (merge L1 and L2, then merge result with L3, etc.) can degrade to O(kN) time, especially when lists are similar in size, while still using O(1) extra space beyond the output.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you compared the strategies well. Now imagine you cannot use extra heap/priority-queue memory beyond O(1), but you still need to merge k sorted linked lists; how would you structure the merges to minimize total time, and what would the resulting time complexity be compared to both the naive sequential merge and the heap-based approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so if I can’t use extra heap memory and must stay O(1) extra space, I’d still just use the basic two-list merge but structure the merges in a balanced, divide-and-conquer way.

So instead of merging L1 with L2, then that result with L3, and so on (which can be O(kN)), I’d repeatedly merge pairs: in each “round” merge (L1,L2), (L3,L4), etc., producing about k/2 lists, then repeat on those results until only one remains. This keeps the merge tree balanced, giving time O(N log k), similar to the heap-based approach, but without the O(k) heap; the trade-off is that you’re doing more manual bookkeeping and only using the in-place two-list merge.

topic: Search a 2D matrix for a target value.

For a mid index, I map it back to 2D as row = mid / n and col = mid % n, compare matrix[row][col] with the target, and adjust the search range accordingly. That gives time complexity O(log(m*n)) and space complexity O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the matrix still has each row sorted and each column sorted, but it no longer has the property that the first element of a row is greater than the last of the previous row. Given that, how would you search for a target value efficiently, and why does your approach achieve that time complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Okay, so with rows and columns both sorted, I’d use the staircase search from a corner. For example, start at the top-right element. If the current value is equal to target, return true. If it’s greater than target, move left (since everything below is even larger). If it’s less than target, move down (since everything to the left is smaller). Each step strictly decreases either the column index or increases the row index, so in the worst case you do at most m + n steps. That gives O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space.

topic: Find minimum window substring containing all characters of another string.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

topic: Find the first missing positive integer in an unsorted array.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the first missing positive integer in an unsorted array, and what time and space complexity would you aim for? Please outline the high-level idea before going into details.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so I’d probably just sort the array first and then scan through it. After sorting, I’d start from the beginning and look for the first positive number, say that’s x, and then I’d just check linearly for the first gap in the sequence of positives. So if I see 1, 2, 3, 5, I’d say 4 is the first missing positive. If the first positive isn’t 1, then the answer is just that first positive minus 1. Sorting is O(n log n), and then the scan is O(n), and I’d say that’s optimal here, with constant extra space since sorting can be done in-place.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear, but the expected solution here is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, so sorting is more expensive than needed. Can you think of a way to use the array itself as a kind of hash structure, rearranging elements in-place so that each positive integer k (if present) ends up at index k-1, and then use that to find the first missing positive?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Ah, okay, so using the array as a hash… I think I’d just loop once and, whenever I see a positive number k, I’d write it directly into position k in the array. So like, if I see a 4 anywhere, I’d put it at index 4. If that position is already occupied, I’d just overwrite it, since we only care that 4 appears somewhere “around” index 4. I’d do this in one pass without swapping back and forth, just assigning nums[k] = k whenever k is in range. After that pass, I’d do another linear scan from index 1 onward and the first index i where nums[i] != i would mean i is the first missing positive.
