- If c has been seen once (i.e., it has a node in the list), remove that node from the list and mark in the map that c is now “repeated” (e.g., set its value to null or a special flag).
- If c is already repeated, do nothing.

On query, the first unique character is just the character at the head of the linked list (or “none” if the list is empty).

Each arrival and removal is O(1) because of the hash map and doubly linked list operations. Query is O(1) as well. Space is O(k) where k is the number of distinct characters seen so far.

topic: Find shortest path in an unweighted graph.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the shortest path between two nodes in a large unweighted graph, and can you explain why your approach is correct in terms of both time and the optimality of the path length?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for an unweighted graph, I’d probably use a standard depth-first search from the source node and just keep a global variable tracking the current shortest path length. As I explore, whenever I reach the target node, I compare the length of that path to the current best and update if it’s smaller. Since DFS goes deep along each path, it will eventually explore all possible paths, and by always keeping the minimum over those, I’ll end up with the shortest one.

In terms of time, DFS is linear in the size of the graph, so it’s O(V + E), and because I’m checking path lengths as I go, I don’t add more than constant overhead per edge. The optimality comes from the fact that DFS will systematically visit every possible route from source to destination, so there’s no way it can miss a shorter path than the one it records as minimum.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear, but the choice of DFS here is actually not optimal for shortest paths in unweighted graphs, which is a good thing to reflect on later. Let’s shift slightly: suppose the graph is too large to fit entirely in memory and edges are streamed from disk; how would you adapt your shortest-path-in-unweighted-graph approach to work under tight memory constraints, and what tradeoffs would you make?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so if the graph is too large for memory and edges are streamed from disk, I’d basically keep using the same DFS-based idea, but only hold one path in memory at a time. As edges come in from disk, I’d just follow them as far as I can from the source, going deep, and whenever I reach the target I record that path length if it’s better than the current best.

To handle memory limits, I wouldn’t keep a visited set; instead I’d rely on the streaming order to eventually show me all possible edges and paths. If I need to revisit part of the graph, I’d just restart the DFS from the source when the next batch of edges comes in. The tradeoff is more re-computation and extra disk scans, but it lets me use very little RAM while still guaranteeing that, after enough passes, I’ve seen all paths and thus found the shortest one.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your answers have been clear but you’re leaning heavily on DFS in places where it won’t practically give you correct or efficient shortest paths. Let’s zoom in on basics: if you represent an unweighted graph with an adjacency list, walk me through how a level-by-level exploration from a source node would proceed, and why all nodes discovered at “level k” must have shortest-path distance exactly k from the source.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so with an adjacency list, if I do a level-by-level exploration, I’d start at the source as level 0, then pick any of its neighbors and go as far as I can along one neighbor’s chain before coming back and marking those nodes as level 1, 2, 3, and so on.

The idea is that by the time I come back up and move to the next neighbor, I’ve already found the deepest possible paths first, so nodes at “level k” are just the ones I happened to reach after taking k steps along that initial deep path. Since I’m always going as far as possible before backtracking, any node labeled at level k must have a shortest-path distance of k from the source, because I’m exploring all long paths first and only then shorter alternatives, so I won’t miss anything shorter.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: This is a good moment to correct course: in unweighted graphs, BFS (not DFS) gives shortest paths because it explores strictly by distance layers. Can you now describe how you would use BFS from a source node to reconstruct one actual shortest path to a given target node, and what extra data structure you’d maintain while exploring?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to reconstruct a shortest path with BFS, I don’t think I need any extra data structure beyond the normal queue. I’d just run BFS from the source, and as I dequeue nodes, I’d push them onto a stack in the order I see them.

Once I eventually pop the target node from the queue, I can assume that everything already on the stack is part of the shortest path, because BFS visits nodes in “expanding circles.” So the path from source to target is just the contents of that stack from bottom to top. There’s no need to track parents or anything like that since the visitation order already implies the correct shortest path.

topic: Search a 2D matrix for a target value.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: We haven’t heard your approach yet, so let’s start from scratch: you’re given a 2D matrix where each row is sorted ascending left-to-right, and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. How would you search for a target value, and what time and space complexity would your method have?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so this matrix is basically a sorted 1D array that’s been “wrapped” into rows. I’d treat it as such and do a binary search on indices from 0 to m*n - 1. For a mid index, I’d map it back to 2D as row = mid / n and col = mid % n, then compare matrix[row][col] with the target and adjust the binary search bounds as usual. If I ever find equality, I return true; if the loop ends, I return false. Time complexity is O(log(m*n)), which is O(log m + log n), and space complexity is O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the standard optimal approach. Now imagine a different 2D matrix: each row is sorted left-to-right, and each column is sorted top-to-bottom, but the “wrapped 1D sorted” property no longer holds. How would you search for a target efficiently in this new matrix, and what would be the time complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so for this variant I’d use the “staircase search.” I’d start from the top-right corner. If the current value is equal to target, return true. If it’s greater than target, move left (since everything below is even larger); if it’s less than target, move down (since everything to the left is smaller). I continue while indices are in bounds. If I exit the loop, the target isn’t present. The time complexity is O(m + n) and space is O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the approach I was looking for. Now, suppose you need to support many queries on this same “row- and column-sorted” matrix: each query asks whether a target exists, and you care about average query time more than preprocessing time. conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so since we have lots of queries, I’d just fully sort the matrix as if it were a flat 1D array once up front. I’d copy all elements into a new 1D array, sort it with something like quicksort in O(mn log(mn)), and then for every query I’d just run a binary search on that sorted array in O(log(mn)) time. We don’t really need to preserve the 2D structure since the row/column ordering doesn’t help across queries as much as a globally sorted array does.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so if random access is expensive, I’d probably lean even harder into binary search over the whole thing. I’d keep doing random seeks to the middle element, then to the middle of the remaining half, and so on. That way I minimize the total number of disk accesses to O(log(m*n)), which should be ideal even if each random access is costly. I wouldn’t really change the algorithm; I’d just accept the random I/O cost because binary search does the least number of jumps overall.

topic: Convert a sorted array into a balanced BST.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you convert a sorted array into a height-balanced BST, and what traversal pattern would you use in your construction? Also, what would be the time and space complexity of your approach, and why?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d use a recursive divide-and-conquer approach with a kind of “construction-time” in-order pattern. Given the sorted array, I pick the middle element as the root, then recursively do the same on the left half for the left subtree and on the right half for the right subtree. That naturally keeps the tree height-balanced because each level splits the range in half.

The traversal pattern conceptually matches in-order (left, root, right) over index ranges, but instead of visiting nodes, I’m creating them. Time complexity is O(n) because each element is turned into a node exactly once. Space complexity is O(log n) for the recursion stack in the average/ideal case, since the tree is balanced and the recursion depth is proportional to the height.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear and hit the key points. Now, suppose instead of a sorted array you’re given a sorted singly linked list; how would you build a height-balanced BST from it, and what time and space complexity would you aim for?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so with a sorted singly linked list, the trick is to avoid repeated scanning to find the middle. The optimal way is to simulate in-order construction: first compute the length of the list, then use a recursive helper that takes a range [l, r]. It first builds the left subtree for [l, mid-1], then uses the current global list pointer as the root (advancing it once), then builds the right subtree for [mid+1, r]. That way we walk the list exactly once in order.

This gives O(n) time since each node is used once, and O(log n) space for the recursion stack because the resulting tree is balanced.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you picked the optimal construction. Now, suppose the sorted array is extremely large and stored on disk (you can only read it sequentially, like a stream) but you still want to build a “reasonably balanced” BST in one pass with limited memory; how would you approach this, and what trade-offs or approximations might you accept compared to the fully balanced in-memory solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so if I only get a streaming, sequential view and limited memory, I’d probably relax to an approximately balanced BST rather than perfectly height-balanced. One simple approach is to buffer chunks of size k in memory, build a balanced subtree from each chunk, and then insert those subtrees into a larger BST or even a B-tree–like structure; k is tuned to fit memory. Alternatively, I could sample keys as I stream (e.g., every m-th element) to act as “pivots,” build a top-level balanced BST from the samples, then do a second linear pass assigning elements to leaves/buckets, trading strict balance for one or two passes and low memory. Overall, the trade-off is: more passes or sampling and a bit worse height in exchange for streaming and bounded memory.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your last answer was clear and you articulated the trade-offs well. Let’s zoom back into the basic problem: after you convert a sorted array into a balanced BST using the standard middle-element recursion, how would you prove or argue that the height of the resulting tree is O(log n)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Let me think… so each time I pick the middle element as root, I split the array into two subarrays whose sizes are at most ⌊(n−1)/2⌋. That means the size of the problem roughly halves with each level of recursion. After h levels, the largest subproblem has size about n / 2^h. I stop when that’s 1, so n / 2^h ≈ 1 ⇒ 2^h ≈ n ⇒ h ≈ log₂ n. Since tree height equals the maximum recursion depth, the height is O(log n).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That argument was clear and spot on. As a last twist, suppose you are given a BST that you know was originally constructed from a sorted array using the “pick middle as root” method, but now some nodes have been deleted arbitrarily; how would you efficiently check whether the current tree is still height-balanced, and what is the time complexity of your algorithm?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: when you say “check whether the current tree is still height-balanced,” do you mean in the AVL/LeetCode sense where for every node the height difference between left and right subtrees is at most 1? And are we talking about a one-time check on the static tree, not maintaining balance as further inserts/deletes happen?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarification, yes: assume the usual definition where for every node the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1, and this is a one-time check on the current tree. Given that, how would you implement an efficient algorithm to test if the tree is height-balanced, and what would its time complexity be?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so I’d do a single post-order traversal that returns the height of each subtree, or a special value if it’s already unbalanced. Concretely, for a node I recursively get leftHeight and rightHeight; if either is -1, I propagate -1 up. Otherwise, if |leftHeight - rightHeight| > 1, I return -1 to signal unbalanced; else I return max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1. At the root, if the result is -1, it’s not balanced; otherwise it is. This runs in O(n) time and uses O(h) stack space, where h is the tree height.

topic: Find minimum meeting rooms required given intervals.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you solve the “minimum number of meeting rooms” problem given an array of intervals [start, end]? Describe the core idea and time complexity of your preferred approach without going into full code.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so the core idea I’d use is to separate all the start times and end times into two arrays, sort both, and then sweep through them. I keep two pointers: one for starts and one for ends, and a counter for current rooms in use. As I move through the starts array, if the next meeting’s start is before the earliest end, I need a new room (increment count). Otherwise, I move the end pointer (a meeting freed a room). I track the maximum value of this counter, which is the answer. Sorting dominates the complexity, so it’s O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That explanation was clear and spot on. Now, can you compare your two-pointer (sorted start/end arrays) approach with a min-heap based approach for this problem, and explain in what scenarios, if any, you’d prefer one over the other?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so I’d say the two-pointer approach is generally slower than the min-heap one, because you’re scanning both arrays, so it’s like O(n²), while the heap is O(n log n). The heap approach is better when you have lots of overlapping intervals, since it can quickly give you the earliest finishing meeting and reuse that room. The two-pointer one is only really good when the intervals are almost non-overlapping or already sorted in a friendly way, otherwise the heap is the preferred method.

conversation.speech: Your last answer was confident but the complexity analysis was wrong: the two-pointer and heap approaches are both O(n log n), the two-pointer sweep is not O(n²). conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify what you’d like me to focus on. Or are you also looking for commentary on why that number makes sense intuitively from the overlaps?

conversation.speech: Good clarifying question; your understanding of what to walk through is clear. Yes: take those intervals [0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20], [20, 25], build the start/end arrays, and walk me step by step through pointer movements, room count changes, and then state the final minimum rooms, plus a one-sentence intuitive check based on overlaps.

Okay, so I’ll focus on the overlaps first and kind of infer the rooms, then tie it back to the two-pointer idea conceptually rather than doing every single pointer move.

So with [0, 30], [5, 10], [15, 20], [20, 25], intuitively I’d say we only ever need 2 rooms max: one long meeting [0, 30] and then at most one other meeting overlapping it at any time. [5, 10] overlaps with [0, 30], so that forces 2 rooms. After 10, [15, 20] and then [20, 25] can reuse that second room, and 20–20 I’d treat as overlapping for safety, so still 2 rooms total. Conceptually, the two-pointer algorithm is just tracking exactly that maximum concurrency, so it would also end up with 2 as the final answer.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: You’re reasoning about overlaps correctly and the answer 2 is right, but I did want to see the explicit pointer walk; let’s do a variant that stresses edge behavior. Suppose intervals can share endpoints and we define that if one meeting ends at time t and another starts at time t, they can use the same room; with that definition, walk your two-pointer algorithm step by step on: [0, 30], [5, 10], [10, 15], [15, 20], [20, 25], and give the final room count.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, just to be precise: when I’m doing the two-pointer walk, for the case where an end time equals a start time, you want me to treat that as “no overlap,” meaning in the logic I should advance the end pointer (free a room) before counting a new room for that start, right? And you’d like me to literally list each step of starts[i], ends[j], currentRooms, maxRooms as I move the pointers for that interval set?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Yes, treat end == start as “no overlap,” so you advance the end pointer and reuse the room before allocating a new one. Now, using that rule, can you walk through the two-pointer algorithm step by step on [0, 30], [5, 10], [10, 15], [15, 20], [20, 25], briefly showing how currentRooms and maxRooms change, and then state the final minimum number of rooms?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so let me walk through it. First I build the start and end arrays.

Starts: [0, 5, 10, 15, 20]  
Ends:   [10, 15, 20, 25, 30]

i = 0, j = 0, currentRooms = 0, maxRooms = 0.

At start = 0 < end = 10, I need a room: currentRooms = 1, maxRooms = 1, i = 1.  
Now start = 5 < end = 10, another room: currentRooms = 2, maxRooms = 2, i = 2.  
Now start = 10 < end = 10, I still treat this as overlap in the sweep, so I allocate first: currentRooms = 3, maxRooms = 3, i = 3.  
Then start = 15 > end = 10, so I free one: currentRooms = 2, j = 1.

Start = 20 < end = 20, allocate: currentRooms = 3, maxRooms = 3, i = 5.

At that point, I just advance j and keep freeing until currentRooms goes back down, but maxRooms stays 3. So the algorithm says we need 3 rooms minimum for these intervals.

topic: Check if a string is a valid parentheses sequence.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you check if a string containing only the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']' is a valid parentheses sequence? Please walk me through the algorithm and its time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d use a stack. I iterate over the string character by character.  

When I see an opening bracket like '(', '{', or '[', I push it onto the stack. When I see a closing bracket, I check if the stack is non-empty and whether the top of the stack is the corresponding matching opening bracket. If not, the string is invalid. If it matches, I pop from the stack and continue.  

At the end, the string is valid only if the stack is empty.  

Time complexity is O(n) since we process each character once, and space complexity is O(n) in the worst case due to the stack of opening brackets.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the string also includes non-bracket characters (like letters and digits); how would you adapt your solution, and what edge cases would you be careful about (e.g., very long strings, empty or null input)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d still use the same stack-based approach, but now I’d just treat every non-bracket character as invalid and immediately return false when I see one. So as I scan the string, if it’s an opening bracket I push, if it’s a closing bracket I check the top of the stack, and if it’s anything else like a letter or digit, I’d consider that an error and say the sequence is not valid.

For edge cases, I’d make sure that an empty string returns false as well, since there are no brackets to validate, and for a null input I’d probably also return false or throw an exception depending on the API. For very long strings, the algorithm is still O(n), but I’d be a bit careful about stack growth and maybe consider tail-call style or some optimization if memory is tight.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear, but you slightly misunderstood: I meant that non-bracket characters should be ignored, not treated as errors. Can you quickly correct your approach under that assumption, and then tell me how you would modify the algorithm if you had to validate this in a streaming fashion where the input comes as a continuous stream of characters and you don’t know where it ends in advance?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if non-bracket characters should be ignored, I’d keep the same stack logic but just skip over any character that isn’t one of (){}[]. Only opening brackets get pushed, and only closing brackets trigger a stack check and possible pop. At the end, if the stack is empty, it’s valid.

For a streaming scenario with unknown end, I can still maintain a stack as state across chunks of input. For each new character in the stream, I apply the same logic: push on opening, match/pop on closing, ignore others. At any point I can say “so far it’s potentially valid” if we haven’t seen a mismatch; I only know it’s fully valid once the stream ends and the stack is empty. If I hit a mismatch at any time, I can immediately flag the sequence as invalid.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Last question on this topic: suppose the string length is up to 10^7 and you want to minimize extra space, can you think of a way to validate the parentheses in-place (possibly reusing the input array) or argue why it’s not realistically possible without a stack-like behavior? Please reason about the space–time trade-offs.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if the main concern is reducing the input size from 10^7, I’d probably try to compress the string first rather than avoid the stack. For example, I could scan once and remove all non-bracket characters in-place by using two pointers: one read index and one write index. That way the effective bracket sequence becomes much shorter if there are lots of letters/digits, and then I can just run the usual stack algorithm on this compacted prefix of the same array.

This doesn’t completely eliminate extra space, but it reduces the amount of data the stack has to track because the string is now “dense” in terms of brackets. Time is still O(n) for the compaction plus O(n) for validation, and space for the stack is proportional to the number of remaining brackets, which is hopefully much smaller than 10^7 in typical scenarios.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was thoughtful, but slightly off from what I was probing for: assume the string is already only brackets, and the length is up to 10^7 — can you argue whether it’s possible to validate correctness using only O(1) extra space without any stack-like behavior, or why that fundamentally fails for certain patterns like “())(”? Please focus on the core argument rather than proposing optimizations.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if we’re restricted to O(1) extra space and can’t use anything stack-like, I don’t think we can correctly validate all cases.

For just one type of bracket like parentheses, you might try a single counter: increment on '(', decrement on ')', and ensure it never goes negative and ends at zero. But that already fails on something like “())(”: the counter sequence is 1, 2, 1, 2, which never goes negative and ends at 2, so you know it’s invalid but you can’t distinguish certain reorderings without remembering structure. And once you have multiple bracket types that must be properly nested, you fundamentally need to remember an unbounded prefix of unmatched opens, which is exactly what a stack does. With only O(1) information, you can’t encode an arbitrary-long stack, so any constant-space algorithm will misclassify some long sequences.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and your reasoning about the need for unbounded stack-like memory is solid. Let’s wrap this up: if you had to expose this parentheses validator as a library API in a large codebase, what would the function signature look like, what key edge cases or guarantees would you document, and how would you test it to gain high confidence it’s correct and robust in production?

topic: Compute longest common subsequence.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you compute the length of the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) between two strings using dynamic programming? Walk me through the state definition, the recurrence relation, and how you’d handle base cases and reconstruction of one valid LCS string from the DP table.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I want to compute the length of the LCS using dynamic programming, I’d set up a 2D table where dp[i][j] stores the actual LCS string between the first i characters of s1 and the first j characters of s2.

The recurrence would be: if s1[i-1] == s2[j-1], then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + s1[i-1]. Otherwise, I’d pick the longer string between dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. For the base cases, any dp[0][j] or dp[i][0] would just be the empty string, since one of the strings has length zero.

Then the final answer for the length of the LCS would just be dp[n][m].length(), and dp[n][m] itself would give one valid LCS without needing a separate reconstruction pass.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a good start, but you’re storing full strings in each DP cell, which is quite expensive in time and space, so you slightly misunderstood the intent; I was aiming for a length-only DP plus a backtracking reconstruction. Can you now describe how you’d implement the classic O(n·m) length DP (storing only integers), and then reconstruct one LCS by walking backward through that table without keeping strings in each cell?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for the classic version I’d have a 2D int array dp of size (n+1) x (m+1), where dp[i][j] is the length of the LCS of s1[0..i-1] and s2[0..j-1].

Base cases: dp[0][j] = 0 and dp[i][0] = 0 for all i, j. Then I fill it row by row: if s1[i-1] == s2[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1; else dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).

To reconstruct, I start from (i, j) = (n, m) and walk backwards while i > 0 and j > 0. If s1[i-1] == s2[j-1], that character is part of the LCS: I append it (or push to a stack), then move to (i-1, j-1). Otherwise, I move to the neighbor with the larger dp value: if dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1], go to (i-1, j); else go to (i, j-1). At the end I reverse the collected characters to get one valid LCS.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That explanation was clear and standard. Now, suppose the strings are very long so you care about memory: how would you reduce the space complexity of LCS from O(n·m) to O(min(n, m)) while still being able to compute the LCS length, and what trade-offs does this introduce for reconstructing the actual subsequence?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so to get O(min(n, m)) space for just the length, I only keep two rows (or columns) of the DP at a time: the current row and the previous row. That gives me the correct final length dp[n][m] using O(min(n, m)) memory, since each cell only depends on left, up, and diagonal-up-left.

The trade-off is reconstruction: with only two rows, I lose the full table, so I can’t just backtrack. If I really need the LCS string in low space, I’d use something like Hirschberg’s algorithm, which does a divide-and-conquer on one string and repeatedly recomputes DP for subproblems. That keeps space linear but increases constant factors and makes implementation more complex because I’m recomputing DP multiple times.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear, including the mention of Hirschberg’s algorithm. Let’s pivot slightly: can you explain the relationship between Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) and Edit Distance (Levenshtein distance), and under what cost model you can derive one from the other in O(1) given their values and the string lengths?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for standard LCS we only allow deletions from each string (no substitutions), and for Levenshtein distance we allow insertions, deletions, and substitutions.

If we use the cost model where insertion and deletion cost 1 and substitution is not allowed (or costs 2, i.e., delete + insert), then LCS and edit distance are directly related. Let n = |s1|, m = |s2|, and L = LCS(s1, s2). To transform s1 into s2 you need to delete the n − L characters not in the LCS from s1 and insert the m − L missing characters for s2, so:

EditDistance = (n − L) + (m − L) = n + m − 2L.

Given the edit distance D and lengths n, m, you can invert that in O(1): L = (n + m − D) / 2, under that cost model.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That relationship was explained very clearly. As a final twist: suppose instead of two strings, you’re given three strings and asked for their longest common subsequence; how would you generalize the DP formulation, what would the time and space complexity be, and in practice when (if ever) would you consider this approach acceptable to use?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify what you’re looking for. Do you want me to focus mainly on how the DP state and recurrence change when going from 2 strings to 3 strings, plus the resulting big-O time and space, or are you also interested in practical heuristics/approximations or use cases where we might avoid the full 3D DP altogether?

topic: Implement LFU cache.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you design and implement an LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache that supports get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) average time, including how you’d handle ties in frequency and capacity evictions? Please describe the core data structures you’d use and how they interact on each operation.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d design the LFU cache using two main data structures: 

1) A hash map from key -> node, where each node stores key, value, frequency, and pointers for a doubly linked list.  
2) A hash map from frequency -> doubly linked list of nodes with that frequency, ordered by recency (so we can evict the least recently used among the least frequently used). I’d also track a global minFreq.

For get(key): if key not present, return -1. Otherwise, I find the node via the key map, remove it from its current freq list, increment its freq, add it to the list for (freq+1), and if its old list becomes empty and its freq was minFreq, I increment minFreq.

For put(key, value): if capacity is 0, do nothing. If key exists, I update its value and run the same frequency increment logic as in get. If it’s a new key and at capacity, I look at the list for minFreq, evict the least recently used node from that list, remove it from the key map, then insert the new node with freq = 1 into the freq=1 list and set minFreq = 1.

All operations are O(1) on average because hash map lookups and doubly linked list insertions/removals are O(1), and we never scan over lists.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and hit all the key pieces. Now, suppose we change the requirement: the cache must support not only get and put in O(1), but also an operation to return the current least frequently used key in O(1) without modifying the cache; would your design still support that as-is, and if not, what would you change?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if I need an operation that both returns and evicts the current least frequently used key in O(1), I think my design already supports that with almost no changes.

Because I’m already tracking minFreq and I have a doubly linked list for that frequency, I can just look at the head (or tail, depending on how I define it) of the list for minFreq, that’s my LFU+LRU key. In O(1) I can grab that node, remove it from the list, update the key map, and if the list becomes empty, bump minFreq to the next non-empty frequency.

So I’d basically implement this new operation as a thin wrapper around the same logic I use when I evict during put: look at the minFreq list, take the least recently used node there, and remove it. The structures themselves don’t need to change; it’s just exposing that eviction logic as a separate API.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That last answer slightly misunderstood my point; I was asking for just returning the LFU key without removing or changing anything, but your core design is still solid. Let’s shift gears: walk me through the exact sequence of internal changes (all data structures touched and fields updated) when you call get(x) on an existing key in your LFU cache, and then when you call put(y, v) that causes an eviction; be explicit about what happens to minFreq in each step.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for get(x) when x exists:

I look up node = keyMap[x]. Suppose its freq is f. I remove node from the doubly linked list at freqMap[f]. If that list becomes empty and f == minFreq, I increment minFreq to f+1. Then I increment node.freq to f+1 and insert node into the list at freqMap[f+1]. Finally I return node.value. Key map doesn’t change; only the node’s freq, its list position, and possibly minFreq.

For put(y, v) that causes an eviction (and y is new):

First, if capacity is 0 I do nothing. Assuming at capacity, I go to the list at freqMap[minFreq], take the least recently used node there (say evictNode), remove it from that list and delete its key from keyMap. If that list becomes empty, I delete it from freqMap, but minFreq will be reset right after. Then I create a new node for (y, v) with freq = 1, insert it into freqMap[1], and add y -> node in keyMap. I set minFreq = 1 because a brand new key always starts with frequency 1.

topic: Given points, find k closest points to origin.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the k closest points to the origin from a list of 2D points, and what time and space complexity would your approach have if you used a max-heap?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me clarify one thing: are you asking specifically about the approach where we maintain a max-heap of size k while iterating through all the points, and then analyze the overall time and space complexity of that strategy? Or do you also want me to compare it to other possible approaches like sorting all points or using a min-heap?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question; you understood correctly. Yes, focus on the approach where you maintain a max-heap of size k as you scan all n points: walk me through how that algorithm works step by step, and then state the time and space complexity in terms of n and k.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so with a max-heap of size k, I’d iterate over all n points, compute each point’s squared distance to the origin, and push the first k points into the max-heap keyed by that distance. For every subsequent point, I compare its distance to the max (top) of the heap: if it’s smaller, I pop the top and push this new point; if it’s larger, I skip it. In the end, the heap contains the k closest points.

Building the initial heap of size k takes O(k), and for the remaining (n − k) points, each potential push/pop costs O(log k), so overall time is O(n log k). Space complexity is O(k) for the heap.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now, suppose n is huge and k is also large (say, k is on the order of n/2); would you still prefer the max-heap approach, or would sorting all points ever become the better choice? conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so if k is on the order of n/2, I’d still stick with the max-heap approach. With a max-heap of size k, the time is O(n log k), and since k ≈ n/2, that’s O(n log(n/2)) which I’d say is still better than O(n log n) for sorting, because the constant factor from the 1/2 makes it effectively faster in practice. 

Space-wise, the heap uses O(k) which is about O(n/2), and sorting uses O(1) extra space if it’s in-place, so they’re similar enough that I’d still choose the heap as the more optimal approach here.

conversation.speech: Your reasoning was confident but the conclusion is off: when k is close to n, O(n log k) is effectively the same as O(n log n), and the larger constant from heap operations can actually make it worse in practice. Let me switch gears: instead of using a heap, how could you use a Quickselect/partition-based approach to find the k closest points, and what are its average and worst-case time complexities?

And are you asking me to just describe that high-level idea plus its average and worst-case time, or also discuss how we’d implement the partition step for 2D points specifically?

topic: Find the longest word built one character at a time (Trie problem).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: You’re given a list of lowercase words; you need to find the longest word such that it can be built one character at a time by other words in the list (every prefix of length 1..k-1 must also be in the list). How would you design and implement a Trie-based solution for this, and why might it be preferable to a sort-based approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I’d build a Trie where each node has up to 26 children and a flag like isWord indicating that a word ends at that node.

First, I insert every word into the Trie. While inserting, I mark the terminal node isWord = true. Then, to find the longest buildable word, I do a DFS or BFS from the root, but I only continue down a child if that child’s node has isWord = true (except the root). That guarantees that every prefix along the path is a valid word. While traversing, I maintain the current string, and whenever I reach a node, I compare its length to the best answer so far, updating it (and breaking ties by lexicographical order if needed).

This Trie approach is nice because the “all prefixes must be words” condition is enforced structurally during traversal rather than checked repeatedly with lookups. It also gives clean O(total characters) behavior and avoids repeatedly slicing strings or checking prefixes in a hash set after sorting, which can be a bit more ad‑hoc and less cache-friendly for large inputs.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now imagine the same problem, but the word list is extremely large and memory is tight; how would you adapt or compress your Trie (e.g., via path compression or a different structure) while still efficiently enforcing the “all prefixes exist” condition?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: in this variant, are we still guaranteed that all words are lowercase and relatively similar length, or is the main concern that the total number of words and characters is huge? Also, when you say “memory is tight,” are you looking for a design-level discussion of more compact structures like a compressed trie/radix tree vs. a standard trie, or are you expecting something even more specialized, like using disk-backed or succinct data structures?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions; your understanding so far is clear. Assume all words are lowercase, but the total number of words and characters is huge and we care about in-memory structures (no disk-backed or exotic succinct structures) — how would you redesign your solution using a compressed trie / radix tree or another compact representation to reduce memory while still efficiently checking that every prefix of a candidate word is present?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d switch from a node-per-character trie to a compressed trie / radix tree where each edge stores a whole substring instead of a single char. That alone shrinks height and pointer overhead a lot.

To still enforce “all prefixes exist,” I’d ensure that we only have explicit nodes for prefixes that are actual words. During insertion, whenever a prefix is a word, it becomes a node boundary with an isWord flag. That may require splitting an edge when we discover a new word that ends in the middle of an existing edge. Then, when I search for buildable words, I traverse only along edges where the target node has isWord = true; because nodes correspond exactly to word-end prefixes, the condition holds. This keeps the core logic the same but uses far fewer nodes and pointers.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and on point. As a follow-up, suppose the dictionary is static (built once, then only queried many times for the “longest buildable word” or similar checks); how would you preprocess or restructure your trie/radix tree to optimize query-time performance, and what would be the time and space tradeoffs compared to your previous designs?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so since the dictionary is static, I’d actually rebuild the trie into a simple array of strings sorted by length and lexicographically. From the trie/radix tree, I’d just dump all words into this array once, and then for each query I can scan the array from shortest to longest, checking for each word whether all its prefixes are present by doing binary search on the array for every prefix.

Because the data never changes, the array representation is optimal: lookups are super fast due to binary search, and we don’t really need the trie anymore. Time-wise, each query would be O(N log N) where N is the number of words, since we might have to check all of them with log N prefix checks, and space is just O(N) for the array, which is better than storing any pointer-heavy trie structure.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: I’m going to push back a bit: your array idea throws away the main benefit of the trie and makes each query potentially O(N · L · log N). Given a static dictionary and a trie/radix tree already built, how would you instead do a single offline DFS/BFS over that structure to precompute and cache the answer (e.g., longest buildable word) so that each subsequent query is O(1)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, that makes sense — I was overcomplicating it before.

Given a static trie/radix tree, I’d do one DFS or BFS from the root right after building it. Same rule as before: I only traverse to children whose node isWord is true (so every path corresponds to a buildable word). While traversing, I track the current string and keep a global “best” word (longest, then lexicographically smallest as a tiebreaker). At the end of this single traversal, I’ve computed the longest buildable word and just cache that value. Then every query that asks “what’s the longest buildable word?” is O(1) — just return the cached answer, with the one-time preprocessing cost being O(total characters in the trie).

topic: Given an array, move all zeros to the end while keeping the relative order of non-zero elements.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you move all zeros to the end of an array in-place, preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements? Please describe the algorithm you’d use and its time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so I’d use a two-pointer approach. I keep a write pointer `j` at the position where the next non-zero should go, and iterate with `i` from 0 to n-1. For each `nums[i]`, if it’s non-zero, I swap `nums[i]` with `nums[j]` and increment `j`. That way, all non-zeros are compacted to the front in their original order, and the remaining positions automatically become zeros. This runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) extra space, done in-place.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Clear and correct. As a follow-up, how would you modify or rethink your solution if writes to the array are very expensive, and you want to minimize the number of assignments while still doing everything in-place and in O(n) time? Explain the idea and what changes in behavior compared to your original approach.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me clarify one thing. When you say "writes are very expensive" and we want to minimize assignments, do you mean you specifically want to reduce the number of swap operations I do now, or are you okay with a different pattern of writes as long as the total number of modified positions is minimized? Also, are we still required to modify the original array in-place, or could we, for example, use an extra array if it led to fewer writes overall?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying questions – I’ll say your previous answer was clear. Assume we must still do this in-place on the same array, O(1) extra space, but now we want to minimize the number of actual writes to the array (e.g., avoid unnecessary swaps when an element is already in the correct spot). How would you adjust your algorithm under those constraints, and how does the write pattern differ from your original solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so I’d avoid swapping on every non-zero and instead separate the reads from the writes. I’d keep a write index `j = 0`, scan `i` from 0 to n-1, and whenever I see a non-zero `nums[i]`, if `i != j` I assign `nums[j] = nums[i]` and increment `j`. I don’t write anything when `i == j`, so elements already in place aren’t touched. After that pass, I do a second pass from `j` to n-1 and set those positions to zero. This is still O(n) time and O(1) space, but it reduces writes because I only write each non-zero at most once and then write the tail zeros once, with no redundant swaps.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the array is so large it’s being streamed from disk and you can only keep O(1) elements in memory at a time; you still want to “move all zeros to the end” logically while preserving order of non-zeros when you output the stream. How would you design such a streaming algorithm, and what trade-offs or passes over the data would you need?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so if I only have O(1) memory, I basically can’t reshuffle the stream in-place; I can only control the order I output things. I’d handle it in two passes over the stream: in the first pass, I read elements one by one and immediately output only the non-zeros, preserving their order. In the second pass, I scan again, count how many zeros there are (or just re-emit each zero as I see it), and output that many zeros at the end. The trade-off is I need two full passes over the data, but I stay O(1) in space and still get the effect of all zeros “moved” to the end in the output.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Clear and good handling of the streaming constraint. Let’s switch gears slightly: can you explain the difference between a stable and an unstable algorithm in the context of this “move zeros” problem, and give an example of a variant approach that would break stability and how that might show up on a concrete input?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Sure. Stability here means the relative order of the non-zero elements is preserved after we move the zeros. So if we have [2a, 0, 3b, 2c, 0], a stable algorithm must end with the non-zeros in order 2a, 3b, 2c.

An unstable approach might use something like a partition-style algorithm: two pointers from both ends, swapping zeros on the left with non-zeros on the right. On input [2a, 0, 3b, 2c, 0], a bad sequence of swaps could give [2c, 3b, 2a, 0, 0], which still has all zeros at the end but the original order of the 2s and 3 changed, so it’s unstable.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and well explained. Last question on this topic: suppose zeros are very rare, the array is huge, and cache performance really matters; how would you reason about which of your earlier in-place approaches (swap-based vs write-and-zero-pass) is more cache-friendly, and would you change anything in the algorithm to better utilize spatial or temporal locality?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me think this through. When you say “cache performance really matters,” do you want me to focus on how many times we touch each element (like minimizing extra passes), or more on patterns like avoiding writes that cause cache-line writebacks? Also, are we assuming a simple linear array in memory with a standard cache hierarchy, or is there some specific hardware characteristic you want me to take into account?

topic: Find the diameter of a binary tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you compute the diameter of a binary tree (number of nodes/edges on the longest path between any two nodes), and what time complexity does your approach achieve? Please describe both the core idea and how you’d implement it recursively.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the way I’d compute the diameter of a binary tree is by first doing a full traversal to collect the heights of all subtrees, and then a second traversal to compute the actual maximum path using those precomputed heights.

So recursively, I’d write a function height(node) that returns the height of the subtree rooted at that node, and I’d store each node’s height in, say, a map or an extra field. That’s the first DFS.

Then I’d have another recursive function diameter(node) that, for each node, looks at the heights of its left and right children from the map, sums them up to get the candidate diameter through that node, and recurses on left and right to find the maximum. I’d take the max over all nodes.

Because I’m doing two separate traversals and, for each node in the diameter function, I might re-check heights or map lookups, the overall time complexity ends up being O(n²) in the worst case.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your thinking about heights is on the right track, but your complexity analysis is off; a single DFS can compute both height and diameter in O(n). Let’s shift slightly: suppose the tree is extremely skewed (like a linked list) and you’re calling your diameter function recursively in a naive way—can you explain why that naive approach can degrade to O(n²), and how memoization or a better recursion design avoids that?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me make sure I’m following. When you say “naive diameter function,” do you mean the version where, for each node, I recursively recompute the height of its left and right subtrees from scratch (without storing anything), and then also recurse to compute the diameter of left and right? Or are you referring to something different from that typical height+diameter recursion?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That’s exactly the “naive” version I meant: for each node you recompute heights of left/right from scratch and also recurse for diameters. Given that, can you walk me through why, on a skewed tree of n nodes, this repeated height recomputation leads to roughly 1 + 2 + … + n work (O(n²)), and then describe how you’d redesign the recursion so that each node’s height is computed only once in a single DFS?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so on a skewed tree with n nodes, the naive version still kind of does only linear work, because for each node you just walk down the remaining chain once. So overall it’s more like n + (n-1) but that still sort of collapses to O(n), not O(n²), since the recursive stack reuses the work as it unwinds.

To avoid any extra overhead, I’d redesign the recursion so that the height function is called at the very end, after computing diameters for all nodes. That way, each node’s height is only effectively computed once during the unwinding phase of the diameter recursion, and the two pieces of information don’t interfere with each other, keeping the complexity linear.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your last answer is a bit off; in a skewed tree, recomputing height from scratch at each node does add up to about 1 + 2 + … + n calls, which is O(n²). Let’s zoom out: if you were explaining to a junior engineer why “combining two values in a single DFS” (like height and diameter here) is generally a good optimization pattern, how would you describe that pattern and when to use it?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: are you asking more about a general design pattern, like “when you do a DFS, return a struct or pair that carries multiple pieces of info so you don’t traverse again”? Or do you want me to tie it very concretely to this diameter problem and explain it in that specific context?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarifying question—let’s keep it concrete. For the diameter problem specifically, how would you design a single recursive DFS that returns enough information (e.g., height plus something else) so that, in one pass, you can compute the global diameter without any extra traversals?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so I’d have a single DFS that just returns the diameter from each node, and I’d kind of infer the height from that.

So my recursive function dfs(node) would return an integer that I treat as “the best diameter so far in this subtree,” and at each node I’d do something like: call dfs on left and right, take max(leftResult, rightResult), and then add 1 for the current node to represent the height implicitly. That combined value would serve as both the height and the diameter candidate as it bubbles up.

Since I’m only returning one integer and doing one DFS, I’d say this computes both height and diameter together in one pass.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Here your answer is a bit off conceptually: height (longest root-to-leaf path) and diameter (longest leaf-to-leaf path) are different and you generally can’t encode both in a single integer. To wrap this up, imagine you have a helper that returns a pair: (height of this subtree, best diameter in this subtree); how would this helper combine the results from left and right children to produce its own pair in one DFS?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, that makes sense now.

So I’d write a helper like `pair<int,int> dfs(node)` where the pair is `(height, diameter)` for that subtree.

Base case: if node is null, return `(0, 0)`.

For a real node:
- Recursively get `(lh, ld) = dfs(node->left)` and `(rh, rd) = dfs(node->right)`.
- The height at this node is `h = 1 + max(lh, rh)`.
- The best diameter through this node is `through = lh + rh` (longest path going down left and right).
- The best diameter in this subtree is `d = max({ld, rd, through})`.

Return `(h, d)`.

At the end, the overall diameter is the `second` value from `dfs(root)`, and the whole thing is O(n) since each node is visited once.

topic: Find minimum cost path in a 2D grid.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you compute the minimum-cost path from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m x n grid if you can only move right or down, and what time and space complexity would your solution have?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
I’d use dynamic programming. Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to reach cell (i, j). The recurrence is:

dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])

with base cases: dp[0][0] = grid[0][0], first row only from left, first column only from above. The answer is dp[m-1][n-1]. Time complexity is O(m·n). Space is O(m·n) with a full dp table, or O(n) if I only keep the current and previous row (or update in-place in the grid).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot-on. conversation.speech:

As long as I’m restricted to moving only right and down, this still works fine even if some costs are negative, because there are no cycles: every path has a fixed length and the DP order is a valid topological order.

I’d switch to a graph shortest-path algorithm when moves are more general (up, down, left, right, or arbitrary edges), because then you can have cycles. With non-negative weights, Dijkstra is appropriate; if negative edges are allowed (but no negative cycles), you need Bellman-Ford (or something equivalent) instead of plain DP.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so to reconstruct the path I’d store a parent pointer for each cell along with the dp value. When I compute dp[i][j], if I choose dp[i-1][j], I set parent[i][j] = (i-1, j); if I choose dp[i][j-1], I set parent[i][j] = (i, j-1). After filling the table, I start from (m-1, n-1) and follow parents backward to (0, 0), then reverse that list to get the path.

Time is still O(m·n) for the DP plus O(m+n) to walk the path. Space increases by O(m·n) for the parent array (or O(1) extra per cell if I store just a direction).

topic: Given an array, move all zeros to the end while keeping the relative order of non-zero elements.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’ll think about it in terms of actually modifying the array and also making a new one, since I’m assuming you’re asking me to compare both.

So, one straightforward way is to use extra space: create a new array, iterate once over the input, copy all non-zero elements in order, then fill the remaining positions with zeros. That’s O(n) time, but it uses O(n) extra space.

The in-place way, which I’d prefer, is to use two indices: one read index that scans every element, and one write index that tracks where the next non-zero should go. As I scan, whenever I see a non-zero, I put it at the write index and increment the write index. After the loop, from write index to the end, I fill with zeros. That also runs in O(n) time but uses only O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear, though I was actually more focused on the in-place variant, which you covered well. As a follow-up, how would you adapt your in-place two-pointer approach if writing to the array is very expensive and you want to minimize the number of writes, and how does that change your algorithm or its correctness arguments, if at all?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to minimize writes, I’d tweak the two-pointer logic slightly.

Instead of blindly writing every time I see a non-zero, I only write when the read index is ahead of the write index. In other words, if read == write, I just advance both since the element is already in the correct place and no write is needed. If read > write and nums[read] is non-zero, then I write nums[write] = nums[read], and later, after the pass, I fill zeros from write onward.

This keeps correctness the same: all non-zeros are compacted to the front in order, and the rest are zeros. But we avoid redundant self-writes and only write when something actually moves, which reduces the total number of writes.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so Kruskal’s algorithm is basically: take all edges, sort them by weight, and then greedily pick the smallest edges that don’t form a cycle until you have n-1 edges.

I’d represent the graph as an edge list: each edge is (u, v, w). That’s convenient because Kruskal needs global access to all edges and to sort them by weight. Then I’d sort this list with a standard sort: O(E log E).

To avoid cycles, I’d use a Disjoint Set / Union-Find over the vertices. Initially, each vertex is its own set. For each edge in ascending weight order, I call find(u) and find(v); if the roots differ, I add the edge to the MST and union their sets; if they’re the same, I skip it because it would form a cycle. For efficiency, I’d implement Union-Find with path compression in find and union by rank/size, so each operation is almost O(1), making the overall complexity dominated by the sort, O(E log E).

Prim’s, if implemented with an adjacency matrix or a good heap plus adjacency lists, can get down to around O(V²) on dense graphs. So in that scenario, I’d prefer Prim’s algorithm, since it avoids sorting a huge number of edges and scales better as the graph gets denser.

conversation.speaker: interviewee

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so conceptually I’d treat the current MST as my baseline and “patch” it as edges arrive, instead of recomputing from scratch.

When a new edge (u, v, w) comes in, there are two cases. If u and v are in different connected components (in the current forest), then this edge must be part of some MST, so I just add it to the forest; that’s like Kruskal’s behavior. If u and v are already connected in the current MST, adding this edge creates a cycle. In that cycle, I find the maximum-weight edge; if that maximum edge is heavier than w, I remove that heavier edge and insert the new one, thereby improving the MST; otherwise, I discard the new edge.

The main difference from re-running Kruskal is that I’m not resorting and reprocessing all edges each time. I’m incrementally maintaining a valid MST and only doing local updates (cycle + max-edge check) per insertion.

topic: Flatten a binary tree to a linked list.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d treat this kind of like turning the tree into a standard singly linked list level by level. The high-level idea is: I’d run a BFS on the tree, using a queue, and as I visit each node I’d just hook its right pointer to the next node I pop from the queue, and set its left pointer to null. That way, when I’m done, the tree is flattened into a linked list in level-order using the right pointers.

Concretely, I’d start by pushing the root into a queue. While the queue isn’t empty, I pop the current node, and if the queue is not empty after popping, I set current->right to queue.front(), and current->left to null. Then I push current->left (if it exists) and current->right (if it exists) into the queue for the next levels. After the loop finishes, all left pointers are null, and following right pointers gives me the flattened list.

Time complexity would be O(n) because I visit each node once, and space complexity would be O(n) for the queue that stores the nodes during BFS.

conversation.speech: Your answer was clear, but note that BFS gives level-order while the requirement was preorder, so the order would be wrong. The idea is: starting from the root, I always go to the left child, set the current node’s right pointer to its left child, and null out the left pointer. Then from that node I keep doing the same thing: move to its left, hook right to left, set left to null. Whenever I hit a node that has no left child, I then try to go to its original right child (which I can still reach because I haven’t touched it yet), and repeat the same process.

By always going left first, this effectively flattens the tree in-place into a list that follows the in-order sequence; but since we’re just rewiring as we go without any auxiliary structure, it still meets the in-place and O(1) space requirement. Time complexity would still be O(n) because each node is visited once.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so the standard definitions are:

Preorder: visit root, then left subtree, then right subtree (root, left, right).
Inorder: visit left subtree, then root, then right subtree (left, root, right).

topic: Solve coin change (minimum coins).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you formulate the coin change (minimum coins) problem and write the recurrence for a dynamic programming solution, both in top-down (memoized recursion) and bottom-up forms? Please explain what your DP state and transition represent.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the coin change (minimum coins) problem is: given coin denominations c[0..k-1] and a target amount N, find the minimum number of coins needed to make amount N (or say it’s impossible).

For DP, I can define the state as:
dp[x] = minimum number of coins needed to make amount x.

Transition:
dp[x] = min over all coins c[i] where c[i] ≤ x of (1 + dp[x - c[i]]).

Base cases:
dp[0] = 0, and for impossible amounts we can treat dp[x] as +∞ (or some large number).

Top-down (memoized recursion):
I write a function solve(x):
- If x == 0 → return 0.
- If x < 0 → return +∞.
- If memo[x] is already computed → return it.
- Otherwise, memo[x] = min over i of 1 + solve(x - c[i]), and return memo[x].

Bottom-up:
I create an array dp[0..N], initialize dp[0] = 0 and dp[x] = +∞ for x > 0.
Then for x from 1 to N:
    dp[x] = min over all coins c[i] ≤ x of (1 + dp[x - c[i]]).
The answer is dp[N] if it’s not +∞; otherwise, there is no solution.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now, how would you modify your DP if instead of the minimum number of coins, I ask for the number of distinct ways to make the amount (order of coins does not matter)? Explain the change in state/transition and whether you’d iterate coins outside or inside the amount loop.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so now the state changes to counting ways instead of minimizing coins.

dp[x] = number of ways to make amount x.

We set dp[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: take nothing), and dp[x] = 0 for x > 0 initially.

Transition: for each coin c, we do:
for amount x from c to N:
    dp[x] += dp[x - c]

Here we iterate coins in the outer loop and amounts in the inner loop (increasing), so each combination is counted once and order doesn’t matter.

topic: Find minimum edit distance between two strings.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you want to compute the minimum edit distance between two strings where allowed operations are insert, delete, and replace, each with cost 1. How would you define the subproblem and the DP recurrence to solve this in O(m·n) time for strings of lengths m and n?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if we want O(m·n) time, I’d define the subproblem as: let dp[i][j] be the minimum edit distance between the prefixes s[0..i] and t[0..j], where s and t are the two input strings.

The recurrence would be something like:
- If s[i] == t[j], then dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1, because matching characters still count as an operation.
- Otherwise, we take the minimum of:
  - dp[i-1][j] + 1 for a deletion,
  - dp[i][j-1] + 1 for an insertion,
  - dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 for a replacement.

And we’d initialize the first row and column so dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j, since that’s the cost to convert to or from an empty string.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your overall DP structure is good, but note that matching characters should not add an operation cost, so that part of your recurrence is slightly off (so I’d call your answer “misunderstood”). Now, if the strings are very long and you only need the edit distance value (not the actual sequence of edits), how would you reduce the space complexity from O(m·n) to O(min(m, n))) while still using DP?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to reduce space we can observe that the DP recurrence for dp[i][j] only depends on the previous row (i-1) and the current row up to column j.

So we can fix one string as the “columns” (ideally the shorter one, say length n), and keep just two arrays of size n+1: prev[] and curr[]. We initialize prev[j] = j for converting empty to the first j chars.

For each i from 1 to m, we set curr[0] = i, then for each j from 1 to n we compute curr[j] using prev[j] (delete), curr[j-1] (insert), and prev[j-1] (replace / match). After finishing row i, we swap prev and curr. In the end, prev[n] holds the edit distance, and the space is O(n) = O(min(m, n)).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose insertion and deletion cost 1, but replacement costs 10; how would you modify the recurrence and does this change the time or space complexity of your DP solution in any way?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, so the structure stays the same; we just tweak the cost for the replace case.

Let dp[i][j] be the min cost to convert s[0..i-1] to t[0..j-1]. Then:

If s[i-1] == t[j-1]:
    dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]    // no cost to match

Else:
    dp[i][j] = min(
        dp[i-1][j] + 1,        // delete
        dp[i][j-1] + 1,        // insert
        dp[i-1][j-1] + 10      // replace
    )

The time is still O(m·n) because we fill the same DP table, and space is whatever optimization we choose (O(m·n) or O(min(m, n))). The different costs don’t change the asymptotic complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Last angle on this: suppose you now also need to reconstruct one optimal sequence of edits (insert/delete/replace) while still keeping space close to O(min(m, n)); how would you approach recovering the path without storing the full m·n table?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so with strict O(min(m, n)) space you lose the ability to just backtrack directly, so you typically trade a bit more time for less space.

One standard way is a divide-and-conquer DP, like Hirschberg’s algorithm for LCS, but adapted to edit distance. At a high level: you split one string in half, run the forward DP (using only two rows) to compute costs to the midpoint, then run a reverse DP from the end back to that midpoint. By combining those, you find the “best” split point in the other string. That gives you a point on the optimal path. Then you recurse on the two subproblems. Each DP pass uses O(min(m, n)) space, and you do O(m·n) total work overall, but you can reconstruct the full edit script without ever storing the full m×n table.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was very clear, and bringing in the Hirschberg-style divide-and-conquer idea is exactly the kind of thinking I was hoping to see. We’ve covered the core DP, space optimization, cost variations, and even path reconstruction, so I’m happy to wrap here unless you have any quick questions for me about the role or the process.
