topic: Given a rotated sorted array, search for a target value.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you have an array that was originally sorted in ascending order, then rotated at some unknown pivot, and you need to search for a target value in O(log N) time. How would you modify binary search to handle the rotation, and what key condition do you use at each step to decide which half to discard?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d still use binary search, but at each step I check which half of the array is actually sorted.

Given mid, I compare nums[left] and nums[mid]. If nums[left] <= nums[mid], then the left half [left..mid] is sorted. Otherwise, the right half [mid..right] is sorted.

If the left half is sorted, I check if target is between nums[left] and nums[mid]. If it is, I move right = mid - 1; otherwise I move left = mid + 1. Symmetrically, if the right half is sorted, I check if target is between nums[mid] and nums[right] and keep or discard that half accordingly. This keeps the search O(log N).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose the rotated sorted array can contain duplicates (e.g., [2,5,6,0,0,1,2]) and you still need to search for a target; how does the presence of duplicates break your previous logic, and what change would you make to handle this while discussing the impact on time complexity?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so duplicates break the logic where I use nums[left] <= nums[mid] to decide which half is sorted, because if nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], I can’t tell which side is properly sorted.

To handle that, when nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right], I can just shrink the range by doing left++ and right-- and continue. In all other cases, I use the same “which half is sorted” logic as before. This keeps correctness, but in the worst case with lots of duplicates (like all elements equal except one), the time complexity can degrade to O(N) instead of O(log N).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and accurate, including the complexity caveat. Now imagine you need not just to search for a target in a rotated sorted array, but to find the index of the minimum element (i.e., the rotation pivot) in O(log N); how would you modify binary search to do that, and how does your logic handle cases with and without duplicates?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so to find the minimum (pivot) without duplicates, I can use binary search with left and right as bounds. While left < right, I compute mid. If nums[mid] > nums[right], it means the minimum is to the right of mid, so I set left = mid + 1. Otherwise, the minimum is at mid or to the left, so I set right = mid. When the loop ends, left (or right) points to the minimum index.

With duplicates, nums[mid] and nums[right] can be equal, which makes it ambiguous. In that case, if nums[mid] == nums[right], I can safely do right-- to shrink the range, since nums[right] can’t be a unique smaller element than mid. This keeps it correct, but like before, in the worst case with many duplicates, it can degrade to O(N).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on, including the duplicate handling. As a follow-up, suppose the array is very large and stored on disk (I/O is expensive) and you only know it is “almost” rotated-sorted: up to k elements may be out of place due to rare write errors; how would you adapt your search strategy or data structure choice to still get good performance, and how would your complexity depend on k?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so pure binary search relies on strict sorted/rotated structure, and with up to k arbitrary errors that guarantee is gone.

One approach is to accept a “local” search around where binary search thinks the target should be. I’d still do a binary-search-style narrowing using the rotated-sorted assumption, but when I land near the expected position, I scan a window of size O(k) around that area to recover from small local disorder. That gives something like O(log N + k) comparisons and, importantly, keeps I/O mostly logarithmic because I only touch O(log N) blocks plus a small contiguous region.

If k is not tiny or the data is mission‑critical, I’d probably instead maintain an index structure (like a B+ tree on the keys) built over the array on disk, so searches are O(log N) I/Os, independent of k, and the “almost sorted” property becomes irrelevant.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a clear answer and I like that you brought in I/O-aware structures. To wrap up, imagine the rotated sorted array is being appended to over time with larger keys (so conceptually it’s a growing sorted array that occasionally gets re-rotated); how would you design a data structure or indexing strategy to support fast searches and amortized-efficient inserts over a long period of time?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if new elements are always larger keys, I’d try not to think in terms of a single rotated array, but in terms of a structure that makes rotation irrelevant.

On disk, I’d probably keep the underlying data in append-only segments and maintain a separate index, like a B+ tree, over the logical key order. Appends just add to the end and insert a new entry into the tree; searches go through the tree in O(log N) I/Os regardless of how the physical array is “rotated.”

If I had to stay closer to an array-like structure in memory, I might use something like a circular buffer of sorted runs plus a small sorted “tail.” Searches first binary search the tail; if not found, binary search the main run using the pivot-aware logic we discussed. When the tail grows too big, I’d periodically merge it into the main run (like a leveled/LSM-tree idea), spreading the rotation/merge cost over many inserts so inserts are amortized efficient and searches stay logarithmic.

topic: Given a grid, find shortest path in binary matrix.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the shortest path in a binary matrix from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, where 0 represents an open cell, 1 represents a blocked cell, and you are allowed to move in 8 directions (including diagonals)? Please walk me through the algorithm you’d choose and its time/space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for this I’d use BFS on the grid, since all moves have equal cost and we want the shortest path in terms of number of steps.

I’d first check if the start or end cell is blocked; if so, return -1. Then I’d run a BFS starting from (0, 0), using a queue that stores the cell coordinates and the current path length. From each cell, I explore all 8 possible neighbors (including diagonals), but only if they’re in bounds, have value 0, and haven’t been visited yet. As soon as I pop the bottom-right cell from the queue, I return its distance as the shortest path length. If the queue empties without reaching it, I return -1.

Time complexity is O(n²) for an n x n grid, since each cell is visited at most once and we check a constant number of neighbors. Space complexity is also O(n²) for the visited structure and the queue in the worst case.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. As a follow-up, suppose the grid is huge and mostly blocked, and the shortest path (if it exists) is very long; how might you optimize or adapt your BFS (e.g., bidirectional search, heuristics like A*) to reduce the search space, and what trade-offs would those introduce?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so a couple of ideas come to mind.

First, bidirectional BFS: run BFS from the start and from the end simultaneously and stop when the frontiers meet. That can drastically reduce the explored area in terms of levels, but you need to maintain two visited sets and it only works cleanly when you know the target and edges are unweighted.

Second, A*: use a heuristic like Euclidean or Chebyshev distance to the goal (since we have 8-directional moves). That prioritizes nodes closer to the goal and prunes a lot of the search space. The trade-offs are you need a good admissible heuristic to keep optimality, and you pay extra overhead for a priority queue and heuristic computation, but in a large, sparse grid it usually explores far fewer nodes than plain BFS.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your explanation was clear. Now imagine each move in the grid can have different costs (for example, moving diagonally costs more than moving horizontally/vertically), and cells still can be blocked; how would you modify your approach to find the minimum-cost path, and what are the key differences in complexity or implementation compared to your original BFS solution?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so once the moves have different costs, plain BFS doesn’t work anymore because it assumes all edges are equal.

I’d switch to Dijkstra’s algorithm on the grid graph. Each cell is a node, each valid move is an edge with its move cost (e.g., 1 for orthogonal, √2 for diagonal or whatever we define). I’d keep a min-heap of (currentCost, cell), pop the smallest, relax all 8 neighbors, and update their distances if I find a cheaper path. Once I pop the bottom-right cell, its distance is the minimum cost.

Time complexity becomes O(V log V + E log V), which on an n x n grid is roughly O(n² log n²), and space is still O(n²) for the distance/visited arrays and the heap. The main implementation differences vs BFS are using a priority queue and storing/relaxing distances instead of simple levels.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot-on. Let’s shift slightly: suppose you are given a huge binary matrix where 0 is open and 1 is blocked, and you need to answer many shortest-path queries between arbitrary start and end cells (not just top-left to bottom-right); how would you design a system or data structure to handle these queries efficiently, and what preprocessing, if any, would you do?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so it depends on how big “huge” is and how many queries we expect.

At the simplest end, if the grid is large but queries aren’t massive in number, I’d just run BFS per query from the given start to end, maybe with a small optimization like early-exit when we hit the target or a bidirectional BFS between start and end.

If we really have tons of queries, full all-pairs shortest paths is too expensive on a big grid, so I’d go for some preprocessing: for example, identify connected components of 0-cells with a flood fill/DFS so I can quickly reject queries where start and end are in different components. Beyond that, for true shortest-path distances, I’d look into more advanced techniques like building a sparse set of landmarks/portals and precomputing distances from every cell to a small set of landmarks, then using those to get good heuristics (A* with landmark-based heuristics) so each query is much faster than raw BFS, trading off preprocessing time and extra memory for lower per-query cost.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you’re thinking about the right trade-offs. Last question on this topic: suppose the grid is not static anymore and cells can flip between 0 (open) and 1 (blocked) over time while you still need to answer many shortest-path queries; how would you adapt your design to handle these dynamic updates without recomputing everything from scratch each time?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so once the grid is dynamic, heavy global preprocessing becomes fragile because a single flip can invalidate a lot of it.

I’d still keep things mostly “on-demand.” For each query I’d run BFS or A* on the current grid state, so updates are just O(1) cell flips. If I did any preprocessing, I’d keep it coarse and easy to maintain: for example, a connected-component labeling that I rebuild lazily in regions that changed a lot, or a small, fixed set of landmarks where I occasionally recompute distance fields in the background. But I’d avoid complex global indices that need to be incrementally updated per cell flip, since that can be more expensive than just re-running a local search for each query.

topic: Find the single non-duplicate element (every element appears twice except one).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: You’re given a sorted array where every element appears exactly twice except for one element that appears only once. How would you find that single element in O(log n) time and O(1) space, and why does your approach work specifically because the array is sorted?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so just to clarify: are you specifically asking for a solution that uses the sorted property with something like a binary search pattern, rather than the simpler XOR linear scan approach? And also, can I assume the array is all integers and strictly follows the “exactly twice except one” rule with no other anomalies?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Great clarifying question – yes, assume all elements are integers and the array strictly follows the “every element appears exactly twice except one” rule, and I do want you to leverage the sorted property (so XOR is not what I’m looking for here). With that in mind, can you walk me through how you’d use a binary-search-like approach to locate the single element, and explain the key invariant you rely on at each step?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d still do something like a binary search, but the key idea I’d use is to compare the middle element with the first and last elements to see which half has a “different” parity of values.

So I’d take mid = (l + r) / 2, and then check if nums[mid] is equal to nums[l] or nums[r]. If nums[mid] equals nums[l], that means the unique element must be on the right side, so I move l = mid + 1. If nums[mid] equals nums[r], then the unique element is on the left side, so I move r = mid - 1. I keep doing this until l meets r, and that index will be the single element.

The invariant I’m relying on is: in the correct half, the boundary elements will always have a matching pair with the middle, while in the half with the unique element, that symmetry breaks, which is why checking mid against the ends tells me which side to discard.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Thanks, that was clear but the logic is actually wrong here, because in a sorted array the middle element usually doesn’t match the first or last element at all. Let me redirect: in a sorted array where pairs are side by side, how does the index parity (even/odd) of elements before and after the single element differ, and how can you use that parity pattern in a binary search to decide whether to go left or right at each step?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, let me make sure I get what you mean by the parity pattern. Are you saying that, in the “normal” part of the array (where everything is still perfectly paired), every pair should start at an even index and end at the next odd index, and that this flips after the single element? Or are you thinking of some other parity rule that I should be checking during binary search?

topic: Find the top view of a binary tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so when you say “top view,” do you specifically mean the set of nodes visible when looking at the tree from above, grouped by horizontal distance from the root, with only one node per vertical line? And are you expecting the output as an ordered list from leftmost to rightmost, or is any container fine as long as the mapping is correct?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Yes, exactly: nodes visible from above, one per vertical line (identified by horizontal distance), and let’s assume the output should be ordered from leftmost to rightmost. With that clarified, describe how you’d implement this: what data structures would you use, how would you assign and track horizontal distances, and why would you choose BFS or DFS here?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d probably do an in-order DFS for this. I don’t think we need to track horizontal distance explicitly. Since in-order already visits the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree, we can just collect the first node we see at each depth and that will correspond to the top view.

So I’d keep an array indexed by depth/level, and during DFS, whenever I reach a level for the first time, I store that node’s value as the visible one from the top. By the time the traversal finishes, that array from smallest level index to largest should give me the top view, left to right.

Can you think about a skewed example, like a tree where the left subtree goes very deep and then has a right child sticking out, and explain why using only level (without horizontal distance) would fail to produce the correct top view?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, I think it would still work. Even in a skewed tree, the in-order traversal is going to visit nodes from the leftmost side up to the rightmost side.

So if the left subtree goes very deep and then has a right child sticking out, that right child will be visited after all the deeper left nodes. Since I’m storing the first node I see at each level, those left nodes at smaller depths will already be recorded, and the later right child at the same or greater depth won’t overwrite them. That should still give me the correct top view ordered by depth, so I don’t see a case where this breaks.

conversation.speech: Got it, I see where you’re coming from, but that logic is still off because “top” is about columns, not depth order. Let me pivot slightly: forget implementation details for a moment and just tell me, conceptually, what’s the difference between the top view and the level order (BFS) traversal of a binary tree?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I’d say they’re basically the same. 

Level order traversal visits nodes level by level from top to bottom, left to right, and the top view is just the nodes you see when you look from the top, which should be exactly the nodes you’d visit first at each level in BFS. So for each level in the level order, those nodes collectively form the top view, since you’re always seeing the “uppermost” nodes as you go down the tree.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That answer is clear but incorrect conceptually; top view picks at most one node per vertical column, while level order can have many nodes per column. Let me wrap this up by quickly explaining: you normally track a horizontal distance (column index) for each node, use BFS with a queue storing (node, column), and record the first node you see for each column in a map, then output from the smallest to largest column as the top view. Thanks for walking through your thinking with me today; we’ll stop here.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Ah, got it, thanks for the explanation. I still feel like we could simplify it though. I don’t really see why we need that horizontal distance or the map at all — if we just did a normal BFS and took all the nodes on the first and last positions of each level, that should already represent what we see from the top, since anything “behind” them on the same level would be hidden anyway.

topic: Solve the Gas Station circular tour problem.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you solve the Gas Station circular tour problem: given two arrays `gas[i]` and `cost[i]`, determine if there is a starting station from which you can complete the circle, and if so, return its index? Please describe both a brute-force approach and then an O(n) solution, and explain why the greedy idea is correct.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so let me define it quickly: at station i you gain gas[i], and it costs cost[i] to go to i+1 (mod n). You want an index s from which you can finish the full circle without gas going negative; if none exists, return -1.

Brute force: For each station s from 0 to n-1, simulate a full lap. Start tank = 0, and walk j from 0 to n-1, updating k = (s + j) % n, tank += gas[k] - cost[k]. If tank ever goes negative, break and try the next s. If you complete n steps without going negative, return s. This is O(n²).

O(n) greedy: First, if sum(gas) < sum(cost), immediately return -1, since total fuel is insufficient globally. Otherwise, there must be at least one valid start.

Then do one pass:  
start = 0, tank = 0. For i from 0 to n-1:
- tank += gas[i] - cost[i]
- if tank < 0, then no station in [start, i] can be a valid start, so set start = i + 1 and reset tank = 0.

After the loop, start is the answer.

Why the greedy reset is correct: If starting at “start” we reach i and tank becomes negative, that means the sum of (gas[k] - cost[k]) from start to i is negative. Any starting point between start and i would have an even smaller prefix sum at i (because you drop some non-positive prefix from the left), so they would also fail by or before i. So when we fail at i, we can safely discard all candidates in [start, i]; the next possible candidate is i+1. Combined with total sum ≥ 0, this guarantees that the final start index can complete the circle.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you justified the greedy step well. Now, suppose the gas and cost arrays are both of length up to 10^5, but instead of returning just one valid starting index, you need to return the total number of starting stations from which you can complete the circuit; how would you do this in better than O(n²) time, and can you outline an O(n) or O(n log n) approach?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so we want to count all valid starting indices, not just find one.

A neat way is to work with prefix sums on the doubled array. Let diff[i] = gas[i] - cost[i]. If total sum < 0, we can instantly return 0. Otherwise, concatenate diff with itself to handle wrap-around, so we have length 2n.

Build prefix sums pref[0..2n], where pref[0] = 0 and pref[i+1] = pref[i] + diff[i]. A start s is valid iff for all k in [s, s + n - 1], the partial sum from s to k is non-negative, i.e. pref[k+1] - pref[s] >= 0. That’s equivalent to min(pref[s+1..s+n]) >= pref[s].

So we need, for each s in [0..n-1], the minimum on the interval [s+1, s+n]. We can precompute all sliding window minimums of size n over pref[1..2n] using a deque in O(n). Call that windowMin[i] = min over pref[i..i+n-1]. Then for start s, we compare windowMin[s+1] with pref[s]; if windowMin[s+1] >= pref[s], s is a valid start.

The whole thing is O(n) time and O(n) space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and the prefix-sum + sliding window min idea is spot on. Let’s zoom out a bit: in your view, what are the key invariants or properties that make greedy algorithms like this Gas Station solution correct, and how do you typically convince yourself that a greedy choice is globally optimal rather than just locally good?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I think about two things mainly: invariants and an “exchange” style argument.

For invariants, like in Gas Station, I maintain something that’s always true as I scan (e.g., total sum so far, and that no index between `start` and `i` can be a valid start once the tank goes negative). If I can state that invariant clearly and it never breaks, that’s a good sign.

Then I usually justify the greedy step by showing that any optimal solution can be transformed into one that makes the same greedy choice without getting worse. That exchange argument (or a contradiction: assume a better solution exists that doesn’t follow the greedy step and derive a conflict with the invariant) is what convinces me the local choice is actually globally optimal.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you articulated the invariant / exchange viewpoint well. Let’s do one last twist on Gas Station: suppose stations are on a line (not a circle), you start with zero gas at station 0, you can choose to skip stations (i.e., not stop to refuel), and your goal is to reach station n−1 with the minimum number of refueling stops; how would you design an efficient algorithm for this and what data structures would you use?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, this is like the “minimum number of refueling stops” problem on a line.

Assume we know the distance between stations and how much fuel each gives. I’d sort stations by position and treat the destination as the last “station” with 0 fuel. Then I scan from left to right, maintaining my current fuel and a max-heap of fuel amounts from all stations I’ve passed but not used yet.

As I move to the next station at distance d, I decrease my fuel by the distance from the previous station. If fuel becomes negative, I repeatedly pop from the max-heap (refuel with the largest available station) and increment the stop count until I have enough fuel to reach this station or the heap is empty. If the heap runs empty and I still can’t reach, it’s impossible. When I arrive at a station, I push its fuel into the max-heap. The max-heap (priority queue) is key to always picking the best previous station to stop at, and this runs in O(n log n).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot-on with the classic heap-based solution. We’ve covered the Gas Station problem and a couple of variants from multiple angles, so I’m good with your understanding and problem-solving approach here — let’s wrap up the interview at this point.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Ah, sure, I thought you wanted me to actually code it out or at least walk through a concrete example, like with specific station positions and fuel amounts, to demonstrate the heap behavior. 

If we had, say, stations at distances [10, 20, 30] with fuels [10, 5, 20] and a destination at 40, I’d start with fuel = 0 and then show how I’d need some initial fuel or a virtual starting station, then simulate the process of pushing each station’s fuel into the max-heap and popping when I can’t reach the next one. That would highlight exactly why the largest previous fuel choice minimizes the number of stops.

topic: Delete a node from a linked list given only that node.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you delete a given node from a singly linked list if you are only given a pointer to that node and you’re guaranteed it is not the tail? Please describe the idea first, then walk through what happens to the data and pointers step by step.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so since we don’t have access to the previous node, we can’t adjust its next pointer directly. Instead, we “replace” the current node’s contents with its next node’s contents. Concretely, we copy `node->next->data` into `node->data`, then we store a temp pointer to `node->next`, set `node->next = node->next->next`, and then free the temp node. Conceptually, we’ve deleted the next node, but from the outside it looks like the original node was removed. This only works because we’re guaranteed the node is not the tail, so `node->next` is valid.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That explanation was clear. Now, what are some edge cases or limitations of this “copy-next-and-delete-next” approach? For example, think about nodes that might be shared, contain large payloads, or have external references to their addresses, and explain when this technique might be unsafe or semantically incorrect.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so a few limitations. First, it doesn’t work for the tail, since there’s no next node to copy from. Second, if other parts of the program hold pointers specifically to the “next” node, they’ll now be pointing to a freed node, which is bad. Also, if the node’s data is large or has identity (like an object with an ID, or reference-counted resources), copying fields instead of actually removing that exact node might break invariants or be expensive. Finally, if the node participates in other structures (like back-pointers or external indices), just copying fields won’t update those other references, so the structure can become inconsistent.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you hit the important limitations. As a follow-up, suppose each node in the singly linked list has an additional “random” pointer that can point to any node in the list (or null); if you still only have a pointer to the node to “delete,” how would you think about the correctness or impossibility of deleting it while preserving list semantics?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so with random pointers it gets a lot trickier. If I just do the copy-next-and-delete-next trick, any external code that was holding a pointer to the original node’s address still sees the same node, but its contents are now those of the next node, which may break invariants about identity. Worse, any random pointers in the list that pointed to the “next” node will now be pointing to a freed node, and I can’t fix those because I don’t have the head or a way to traverse everything. So in a structure with arbitrary external and random references, given only the node, you generally can’t safely preserve full semantics with this trick; it’s not reliably correct.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a clear articulation of why the trick can break down with richer semantics. Last question on this topic: if you were designing a linked list API from scratch in a production system, knowing these pitfalls, what invariants or API constraints would you impose so that “delete given only the node” is always safe and well-defined, and what trade-offs would that introduce for users of the API?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so to make “delete given only the node” safe, I’d design the list with some strict constraints. First, nodes wouldn’t be exposed as stable identities outside the list; users interact via values, iterators, or handles, not raw node pointers. Second, I’d guarantee no extra back-links like random pointers or external indices that aren’t maintained by the list itself. Under those rules, the list owns all references, so internally I’m free to use the copy-next-and-delete-next trick for non-tail nodes, and maybe disallow deleting the tail via that API or provide a different operation for it. The trade-off is less flexibility: users can’t stash and rely on raw node addresses or arbitrary cross-links, but in return they get simpler, well-defined semantics and O(1) deletion given a node handle.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you tied the implementation details back to API design nicely. Let’s wrap on a quick complexity check: for this “delete given only the node (non-tail)” operation in a singly linked list, what are the time and space complexities, and is there any realistic way to do asymptotically better or worse here given the constraints?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Time complexity is O(1) because we just copy the next node’s data and adjust a couple of pointers, and space complexity is O(1) since we only use a temporary pointer. You can’t really do asymptotically better than O(1) here, since that’s already constant time, and given we must at least touch the node we’re deleting and its next, any realistic implementation will also be O(1) in both time and extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and on point. We’ve covered this topic well, so we’ll stop here for now—thanks for walking through the nuances of deleting a node from a linked list given only that node.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Thanks for the questions—this was a fun one to walk through.

topic: Given a matrix, compute number of islands (connected components).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Given a 2D grid of '0's (water) and '1's (land), how would you compute the number of islands, where an island is a group of horizontally or vertically connected '1's? Walk me through your core idea and what data structures you’d use.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so I’d treat this as a connected-components problem on a grid. I’d iterate over every cell; when I see a '1' that hasn’t been visited, I increment the island count and run a DFS or BFS from that cell to mark all connected '1's as visited.

For data structures, I’d use a 2D boolean visited array (or mutate the grid to mark visited cells) and a stack or queue for DFS/BFS. From each land cell, I explore its up/down/left/right neighbors as long as they are in bounds, are '1', and not yet visited. After finishing that traversal, I know I’ve fully explored one island.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now suppose the grid is extremely large and stored in a distributed system where you can only stream rows or chunks and cannot hold the whole grid in memory at once; how would you adapt your island-counting approach to work in this setting, and what trade-offs would you consider?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me make sure I understand the constraints. When you say I can only stream rows or chunks, do I get to define the chunk size and can I revisit previously streamed chunks, or is it more like a one-pass stream where past data isn’t accessible anymore? Also, are chunks guaranteed to be contiguous rows, or could they be arbitrary partitions of the grid?

topic: Compute matrix chain multiplication.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you define the Matrix Chain Multiplication problem, and what is the key subproblem structure that allows a dynamic programming solution instead of a greedy one? Please walk through the recurrence relation and explain what dp[i][j] represents.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the Matrix Chain Multiplication problem is: given a sequence of matrices A1, A2, …, An with dimensions p0×p1, p1×p2, …, p(n−1)×pn, we want to decide where to put parentheses so that the total number of scalar multiplications is minimized.

The key subproblem is that the optimal way to parenthesize A_i…A_j must be composed of optimal solutions to some split A_i…A_k and A_{k+1}…A_j. That optimal substructure is why dynamic programming works, and a greedy choice (like always picking the smallest dimension first) can fail.

We define dp[i][j] as the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product Ai…Aj. The recurrence is:

dp[i][i] = 0 for all i  
dp[i][j] = min over i ≤ k < j of ( dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p_{i-1} * p_k * p_j )

Here p_{i-1}×p_k×p_j is the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices from the split at k.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now, suppose I give you the dimensions array p of length n+1; how would you implement the DP solution iteratively (bottom-up)? Describe the order in which you fill dp[i][j], the time and space complexity, and how you would reconstruct the actual parenthesization, not just the minimum cost.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d do a bottom-up DP over chain length.

We have n matrices, dimensions array p[0..n]. I create two n×n tables: dp[i][j] for min cost, and split[i][j] to store the k that gave that min.

Initialize dp[i][i] = 0 for all i. Then I iterate by length L from 2 to n. For each i from 1 to n−L+1, set j = i+L−1. For this (i, j), I try all splits k from i to j−1 and compute:

cost = dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i−1] * p[k] * p[j]

If cost is smaller than current dp[i][j], update dp[i][j] and record split[i][j] = k.

Time complexity is O(n^3) because of the three nested loops (L, i, k). Space is O(n^2) for dp and split.

To reconstruct the parenthesization, I do a recursive function print(i, j): if i == j, print Ai; otherwise, print "(", then print(i, split[i][j]), then print(split[i][j]+1, j), then ")".

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and complete. Now imagine the dimensions array p is very large (say n up to 10^5), so the classic O(n^3) DP is impossible; how would you think about approximating or restructuring the problem to get something more efficient, and in what practical scenarios would you relax optimality to do so?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify the scope. Are you asking for a fundamentally different algorithm that still tries to minimize scalar multiplications for an arbitrary chain of length up to 10^5, or is this more about practical heuristics/approximations under some real-world assumptions, like specific patterns in the dimensions or streaming/online settings?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarification question, so let’s focus on practical heuristics: suppose n is around 10^5 and you’re implementing a query optimizer that must pick a near-good parenthesization quickly, knowing exact optimal DP is impossible. How would you design a heuristic or approximation strategy (e.g., greedy, local improvements, exploiting patterns in dimensions, or segmenting the chain) and how would you reason about its trade-offs and where it might fail badly?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for n around 10^5 I’d definitely give up on exact DP and do something heuristic but structured.

One idea is a greedy “locally cheapest merge” strategy: look at adjacent matrix pairs, estimate the multiplication cost p[i-1]*p[i]*p[i+1], and repeatedly pick the cheapest merge (like Huffman-style but with this cost). Maintain a priority queue of neighboring pairs, update neighbors when you merge. That runs in roughly O(n log n). It’s fast, but can fail when a locally cheap merge creates very “fat” intermediate matrices that make later costs explode.

To mitigate that, I might combine it with segmentation: break the chain into moderate-size blocks (say a few hundred long), run exact O(m^3) DP within each block, and then run the greedy heuristic across the resulting block-level matrices. Trade-off is you get better local optimality and still remain feasible overall, but you might miss cross-block optimizations. For a query optimizer, that’s often acceptable since you care about “good enough, fast to compute” rather than perfect.

topic: Find the longest palindromic substring.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you find the longest palindromic substring in a given string, and what are the time and space complexities of the approaches you’d consider (including any optimal one you know)?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so the classic approach is to expand around centers. A palindrome is defined by its center, and there are 2n−1 possible centers (each character as an odd-length center, and each gap between characters as an even-length center). For each center, I expand left and right while characters match, and track the longest substring seen.

That runs in O(n²) time in the worst case and uses O(1) extra space.

If we want optimal time, there’s Manacher’s algorithm, which preprocesses the string (often inserting separators) and computes the longest palindromic substring in O(n) time with O(n) space, but it's more complex to implement.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you covered the key algorithms well. Now, suppose I give you a stream of characters (one by one) instead of a fixed string; how would you maintain and report the longest palindromic substring seen so far, and what trade-offs or approximations might you consider for this streaming setting?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for a true streaming model with unbounded input, maintaining the exact longest palindromic substring online is tricky and usually expensive.

One idea is to adapt Manacher-like logic incrementally: as each new character arrives, treat it as extending the processed prefix and update palindromic radii around centers near the end. That works well for palindromes ending at the current position, but the global longest might appear entirely in the middle, so we still need to retain enough history to compare lengths; in practice this means O(n) memory over time.

If we’re okay with approximations, we could limit ourselves to palindromes up to some max length window (say last W characters). Then we only store a sliding window and run center expansion within that, giving us bounded memory O(W) and per-character time around O(W), while possibly missing a longer palindrome that starts before the window.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear; you correctly highlighted the difficulty of exact streaming and the need for windowing or incremental updates. Let’s shift slightly: suppose instead of the longest palindromic substring, I just want to count all palindromic substrings in a given string and maybe also support answering “how many palindromic substrings in s[l..r]?” queries efficiently; how would you design such a solution, and what data structures or preprocessing would you use?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for just counting all palindromic substrings in the whole string, I can reuse the expand-around-center idea or Manacher’s algorithm. Both effectively give me, for each center, the radius of the longest palindrome, and the sum of those radii (adjusted for even/odd) is the total count. That’s O(n²) with expansion, or O(n) with Manacher.

For answering “how many palindromic substrings in s[l..r]?” efficiently, I’d want preprocessing. One option is to run Manacher once, derive all palindromic intervals [L,R], and store them. Then I can build a 2D structure or, more practically, reduce to prefix sums by, say, keeping for each position an array or Fenwick tree of counts of palindromes ending (or starting) there. Range queries are tricky because a palindrome might start before l and end inside [l,r], or vice versa. If I really need fast online range queries, I’d probably look into using a palindromic tree (EERTREE) plus some offline processing over queries, or accept a slower per-query adjustment over precomputed palindromic intervals.

topic: Implement Bellman-Ford algorithm.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you implement the Bellman-Ford algorithm for a directed weighted graph, and what information would you store in your main arrays during relaxation (beyond just the distance)? Please also explain how you’d detect and report a negative weight cycle using your implementation.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so Bellman-Ford works by relaxing all edges |V|−1 times. I’d keep a distance array `dist[]` initialized to ∞ except the source as 0, and a parent/predecessor array `parent[]` to reconstruct paths.

On each of the |V|−1 iterations, for every edge (u, v, w), if `dist[u] + w < dist[v]`, I update `dist[v]` and set `parent[v] = u`.

To detect a negative cycle, I do one extra pass over all edges after those |V|−1 iterations. If I can still relax any edge (i.e., `dist[u] + w < dist[v]` holds for some edge), that means there is a reachable negative weight cycle. To report it, I can follow `parent[]` backwards from that vertex several steps to get into the cycle, then walk again until I come back to the same vertex to list the cycle nodes.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and correct. Now, suppose your graph is large and sparse and you run Bellman-Ford from a source where only a small portion of the graph is actually reachable; how would you optimize the standard implementation to avoid doing useless relaxations, and what would be the resulting time complexity in the best and worst cases?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so one simple optimization is to only process vertices whose distance actually changed in the previous iteration.

I’d maintain a set or queue of “active” vertices. Initially it just has the source. For each active vertex u, I relax only its outgoing edges; if `dist[v]` improves, I add v to the next iteration’s active set. If in some iteration the active set becomes empty, I can stop early.

In the best case, when only a small reachable subgraph is affected and it stabilizes quickly, the time can be close to O(E_reachable), where E_reachable is the number of edges from reachable vertices. In the worst case, if essentially everything keeps getting updated each round, it still degrades to the usual O(V·E).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your last answer was clear. Now, can you compare Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra’s algorithm: in what scenarios would you choose Bellman-Ford even if all edge weights are non-negative, and is there any way to leverage Bellman-Ford (or its ideas) to handle all-pairs shortest paths efficiently on a graph that may contain negative edges but no negative cycles?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if all weights are non-negative I’d usually prefer Dijkstra because it’s faster, but I might still pick Bellman-Ford if I need simpler code on very small graphs, or if I want built-in negative-cycle detection and I’m not entirely sure inputs will always stay non-negative.

For all-pairs shortest paths with possible negative edges but no negative cycles, I’d use Johnson’s algorithm, which basically combines Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra. You run Bellman-Ford once from a super-source to compute vertex potentials, reweight edges to make all weights non-negative, then run Dijkstra from each vertex on the reweighted graph.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and on point. Let’s go a bit deeper: can you sketch how you’d implement Johnson’s algorithm end-to-end, including how exactly you reweight edges using the Bellman-Ford distances and then adjust the final Dijkstra distances back to the original weights?

That way, I cover all permutations formed by pairwise swaps. The time complexity would be O(n²) because of the two nested loops, and space would be O(n²) as well for storing the permutations.

Because a correct algorithm has to actually produce each distinct permutation at least once, it has to do at least O(n!) work just to write them out, so the time complexity of any full-permutation generator is at least Ω(n!).

I’d represent the graph as a list of edges, where each edge is (u, v, w). I’d keep a distance array dist[] of size V, initialized to +infinity, with dist[src] = 0. Optionally, I’d also keep a parent[] array to reconstruct paths, initialized to -1.

The core idea is relaxation. I run V-1 iterations, and on each iteration I loop over all E edges. For each edge (u, v, w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v], I update dist[v] = dist[u] + w and set parent[v] = u. After V-1 passes, if there is no negative cycle reachable from the source, all shortest paths are settled.

To detect a negative cycle, I do one more pass over all edges. If I can still relax any edge (i.e., dist[u] + w < dist[v] for some edge), that means there’s a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.

Time complexity is O(V * E), since I do V-1 (or V) passes over all E edges. To reconstruct the shortest path to some target t, I check that there’s no negative cycle, then walk parent[] backwards from t to src, collecting nodes, and finally reverse that list.

topic: Find minimum number of arrows to burst balloons.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Suppose you’re given a list of intervals representing balloons on a 1D line, where each interval [start, end] is the x-range of a balloon. How would you compute the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons if each arrow is shot vertically at some x and bursts all balloons whose intervals contain that x? First explain the intuition for your approach before mentioning time complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Right, so this is a classic interval problem. Intuitively, if intervals overlap, one arrow can cover all of them if we shoot it somewhere in their common overlap. So the greedy idea is: sort the balloons by their end coordinate, then iterate from left to right, always shooting an arrow at the end of the current interval, and then skipping all subsequent intervals that start at or before that arrow position (since they’re burst by the same arrow). Whenever we find an interval that starts after the last arrow position, we need a new arrow and update the arrow position to this interval’s end. Sorting takes O(n log n), and the single pass is O(n), so overall time is O(n log n) and space is O(1) extra aside from the sort.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly the standard greedy solution. Now, suppose the intervals are so large that they can’t all fit in memory at once and are streamed from disk, but you’re still allowed an external sort; how would you adapt your algorithm or data handling to still compute the minimum number of arrows efficiently, and what complexity tradeoffs would you consider in this external-memory setting?

Since I’m only doing one pass and never revisiting data, I don’t need to sort by end at all.

I/O cost is just O(N) because I read each interval once from disk, and CPU is also O(N) since I’m doing O(1) work per interval. This way I avoid the N log N external sort and still get the minimum number of arrows.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: The last answer is actually incorrect, because without sorting you can’t guarantee optimality when intervals arrive in an arbitrary order. topic: Given two arrays, compute their intersection.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you compute the intersection of two arrays, and what changes (if any) would you make if the arrays are unsorted and can contain duplicates? Please walk through your preferred approach and its time and space complexity.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so if the arrays are unsorted and can contain duplicates, my preferred approach is to use a hash map.

Concretely, I’d iterate over the first array and build a frequency map: for each value, count how many times it appears. Then I’d scan the second array; for each element, I check if it’s in the map with a positive count. If it is, I add it to the result and decrement its count in the map. That naturally handles duplicates correctly.

Time complexity is O(n + m), where n and m are the lengths of the two arrays, because each array is scanned once and hash operations are O(1) on average. Space complexity is O(min(n, m)) for the frequency map and the result.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now suppose the two arrays are each too large to fit in memory at once (think they’re on disk or coming as streams) and you still need to compute their intersection, including handling duplicates correctly; how would you adapt your approach in that external-memory / streaming setting, and what trade-offs would you consider?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if the arrays are coming in as streams, I’d think of them as unbounded or very long sequences rather than focusing on the memory limit of each array.

What I’d do is still build a frequency map for the first stream as it arrives, but I’d apply some kind of sampling or eviction policy once the map grows beyond a memory threshold, so I only keep “recent” or more frequent elements. Then, as the second stream comes in, I’d probe this in-memory map and emit matches, decrementing counts like before to handle duplicates.

The trade-off is that by not storing the entire first stream, I might miss some intersections for elements that appeared earlier and were evicted from the map. But this way I respect the memory constraints and still get a “best-effort” intersection over what I can hold in memory at any given time.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

Think instead of classic external-memory techniques: how would you compute the exact intersection if both arrays live on disk and you can only load chunks, and how would your approach differ if the arrays are already sorted vs unsorted?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, okay, so if both arrays live on disk and I can only load chunks, I’d first try to avoid doing any preprocessing like sorting on disk, and instead assume I can get random access to disk fairly cheaply.

So for the unsorted case, I’d conceptually keep using the hash-map idea, but “paging” it: I’d read a chunk of A into memory, build a hash map for just that chunk, then stream through the entire B on disk, probing that small in-memory map and outputting matches. Then I’d discard that map, read the next chunk of A, rebuild the map, and scan all of B again. That way I never need to hold all of A or B in memory; I just pay more I/O by rereading B multiple times.

If the arrays are sorted on disk, I’d do something similar but still in a chunked way: read a chunk of A and a chunk of B, and do a merge-style intersection on those two chunks, then advance whichever side has the smaller element, loading new chunks as needed. I’m assuming here that rereading or sequentially scanning from disk is acceptable, and I’m not doing an up-front external sort step.

Let’s switch gears: if I now generalize the problem to the intersection of K sorted arrays (K could be large), how would you compute their intersection efficiently, and what time and space complexity would your approach have in terms of total number of elements N and K?

conversation.speech:

So I’d start by intersecting array 1 and array 2 using the standard two-pointer merge-like approach to get a temporary result. Then I’d intersect that result with array 3, then intersect that new result with array 4, and so on until I’ve processed all K arrays.

Each intersection of two arrays of total size up to N would be O(N), and since I’m doing this K times, the total time complexity would be O(N·K). Space-wise, I only need space for the current intermediate result and a couple of pointers, so that would be O(N) in the worst case.

topic: Reorder a linked list: L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1…

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speech: Okay, got it’s in-place and void. conversation.speech: Good that you’re checking constraints; I’ll say your understanding is clear. Let’s target the stricter version: aim for O(1) extra space (beyond a handful of pointers) and O(n) time, so no arrays or stacks of nodes. conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d do it in three main steps.

First, find the middle of the list using slow/fast pointers. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; then I split the list into two halves by doing something like `second = slow->next; slow->next = nullptr`.

Second, reverse the second half in-place using the standard iterative reverse (prev, curr, next pointers).

Third, merge the two halves by alternating nodes: take one from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, rewiring `next` pointers as you go until the second half is exhausted. That produces L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → …

Each step is linear, so overall time is O(n), and I only use a constant number of extra pointers, so space is O(1).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a very clear high-level algorithm. Now imagine you’re coding the merge step: can you walk me through the exact pointer updates you’d do in a loop to weave the two halves together, and how you’d avoid accidentally creating cycles or losing track of the remaining nodes?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so for the merge I’d keep two pointers, say `p1` on the first half and `p2` on the reversed second half. Inside a loop, I’d just do:

`p1->next = p2;`
`p2->next = p1->next;`

Then advance both: `p1 = p1->next; p2 = p2->next;` and keep going while both are non-null. Since I’m always wiring `p1` to `p2` and then `p2` back to `p1->next`, the structure should just alternate correctly until one side runs out, and I don’t really need temporary pointers because I’m always following the updated `next` pointers.

topic: Implement wildcard matching with '?' and '*'.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you implement wildcard pattern matching where the pattern can contain '?' (matches exactly one character) and '*' (matches any sequence of characters, including empty), given an input string s and pattern p? Describe an algorithm that returns true/false for a match and talk through both a straightforward DP solution and how you’d optimize space and handle tricky cases like consecutive '*' characters.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so, I’d treat this like a classic DP over indices of s and p.

The straightforward DP: let dp[i][j] be true if the prefix s[0..i-1] matches p[0..j-1]. Dimensions are (m+1)×(n+1). Initialize dp[0][0] = true. For the first row (i = 0), dp[0][j] is true only if p[0..j-1] are all '*', so dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] && p[j-1] == '*'.

Transition:
- If p[j-1] is a letter or '?': dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] && (p[j-1] == s[i-1] || p[j-1] == '?').
- If p[j-1] is '*': it can match empty or one-more character:
  dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1]  (use '*' as empty)
          || dp[i-1][j]; (use '*' to cover s[i-1])

Answer is dp[m][n]. Time is O(mn), space O(mn).

To optimize space, I only keep two rows (prev and curr) or even a single 1D array dp[j] updated right-to-left for non-* and carefully for '*'. A simpler optimization is to first compress the pattern by merging consecutive '*' into a single '*', since '**' is equivalent to '*'; that cuts unnecessary states and avoids tricky redundant cases. The logic stays the same; we just run DP on the compressed pattern.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on for the DP approach. Now, suppose I tell you we want to avoid O(mn) time and aim for something closer to linear in the lengths of s and p; can you describe a greedy/two-pointer algorithm for this wildcard matching, explain why it works, and how it handles backtracking when a previous '*' needs to absorb more characters?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, let me just clarify what you’re looking for. When you say “closer to linear,” do you specifically mean the classic greedy approach with at most one pass over s and p plus some backtracking on the last seen '*', or are you open to an amortized-linear algorithm that might still do some re-scanning? Also, do you want me to focus mainly on the high-level idea and correctness intuition, or should I walk through edge cases with examples as well?

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Good clarification, and your understanding is on the right track. Yes, I mean the classic amortized-linear two-pointer approach that may backtrack to the last '*'; can you describe how you’d structure the pointers, what extra state you’d keep for the last '*', and how the algorithm proceeds when characters don’t match?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so I’d use two pointers: i for s, j for p. I also keep two extra indices: starIdx = -1 (position of last '*'), and matchIdx = -1 (position in s corresponding to that '*').

Then I scan while i < len(s):
- If j < len(p) and (p[j] == s[i] or p[j] == '?'), I just advance both i++ and j++.
- Else if j < len(p) and p[j] == '*', I record starIdx = j, matchIdx = i, and move j++ (treat '*' as potentially empty for now).
- Else if starIdx != -1, it means I can backtrack to the last '*': I set j = starIdx + 1 and increment matchIdx++, then set i = matchIdx (so the '*' now absorbs one more character).
- Otherwise, it’s a mismatch and I return false.

After the loop over s, I skip any trailing '*' in p (while j < len(p) and p[j] == '*') j++. In the end, return j == len(p). The backtracking is always to the last '*', and each character in s is advanced monotonically, so it runs in linear time amortized.

topic: Find the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech: Hmm, okay, so when you say “subsequence” here, you mean we can skip elements but we have to keep the original order, right? conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Yes, subsequence means you can skip elements but must preserve order, and your clarifying questions were clear. Let’s start with the O(n²) DP: how would you define the DP state, the transition, and the final answer for the length of the longest increasing subsequence?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so for the O(n²) DP, I’d define dp[i] as the length of the longest increasing subsequence in the entire array using elements from index 0 up to i, not necessarily ending at i.

Then the transition would be something like: for each i, I look at all j < i, and if nums[j] < nums[i], I’d do dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j]) because I’m extending the best subsequence I’ve seen so far up to j. After I process all i, the answer would just be dp[n-1], since that represents the best LIS length considering the full array up to the last index.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was a good start but you slightly misunderstood the DP definition: typically dp[i] is “length of the LIS ending at i,” and the final answer is max over all dp[i], not just dp[n-1]. Can you restate the O(n²) solution with this corrected definition, and then briefly outline how the O(n log n) “tails” array changes what dp[i] represents conceptually?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Okay, got it, so dp[i] is the length of the LIS ending at i.

So I’d do something like: initialize dp[i] = 1 for all i, and for each i I look at all j < i. If nums[j] <= nums[i], then I can extend that subsequence, so I set dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1). In the end, instead of just dp[n-1], I’d take the maximum over all dp[i] as the LIS length.

For the O(n log n) version with the tails array, I’m thinking of tails[k] as basically being the same as dp[k], like the length of the LIS ending at position k, but we store it in a compressed way and update it using binary search to keep everything in O(log n) per element.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your DP recurrence is close, though for strictly increasing we need nums[j] < nums[i], and your mental model of the tails array is a bit off: tails[len] is not tied to an index, but is the minimum possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length len+1. With that in mind, can you walk through how you would update the tails array, step by step, as you process each element of an example like [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18], and explain why its size at the end equals the LIS length?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, that makes sense. So with the O(n log n) “tails” approach, we keep an array tails where tails[k] is the minimum possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.

For the example [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]:

- Start: tails = []
- See 10: tails = [10]   (new length-1 subsequence)
- See 9: binary search → replace 10 with 9 → tails = [9]
- See 2: replace 9 with 2 → tails = [2]
- See 5: 5 is greater than 2 → append → tails = [2, 5]
- See 3: binary search → find position of first ≥ 3 (which is 5) → replace → tails = [2, 3]
- See 7: > 3 → append → tails = [2, 3, 7]
- See 101: > 7 → append → tails = [2, 3, 7, 101]
- See 18: binary search → first ≥ 18 is 101 → replace → tails = [2, 3, 7, 18]

We never shrink tails, we only replace elements with smaller ones or append. So its length always equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence we’ve seen so far. At the end, len(tails) = 4, which is the LIS length.

topic: Given an array, find all unique triplets that sum to zero.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: For the "3-sum" problem, can you walk me through an approach that finds all unique triplets summing to zero in O(n²) time, and explain how you avoid duplicate triplets both in terms of values and indices?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so for O(n²) time, I’d actually stick with a straightforward triple loop but prune it. So I’d sort the array first, which is O(n log n), and then use three nested loops, but the innermost loop starts from i+2 and breaks early whenever the sum goes over zero because the array is sorted.

So something like: for i from 0 to n-3, for j from i+1 to n-2, for k from j+1 to n-1, compute sum = nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k]. topic: Find subset sum equal to target.

conversation.speaker: interviewer

The transition is: dp[i][t] = dp[i-1][t] (exclude) OR, if t ≥ a[i], dp[i-1][t - a[i]] (include). Initialize dp[0][0] = true, others false, and at the end check dp[n][S]. That’s O(n * S) time and O(n * S) space, which can be optimized to O(S) space using a 1D array updated from S down to 0.

topic: Implement a basic calculator with + - * / and parentheses.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you implement a basic calculator that evaluates a string expression containing non-negative integers, +, -, *, /, and spaces, but no parentheses? You can assume integer division truncates toward zero; walk me through the core idea and main data structures you’d use.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:

I’d have a variable `result` and a variable `currentNumber`. As I iterate over the string, I build up `currentNumber` whenever I see digits. When I hit an operator like +, -, *, or /, I immediately apply it to `result` with the `currentNumber`. So for example, starting with `result = 0`, if I see “3+5*2” I’d do: read 3, then on `+` I do `result = result + 3` → 3; then read 5, on `*` I do `result = result * 5` → 15; then read 2, and at the end I do `result = result * 2` → 30.

So the main idea is: single pass, no stack, just keep the last operator and update `result` as soon as you see the next operator, regardless of whether it’s +, -, *, or /. That way you never need extra data structures, just a few integers and the last seen operator.

conversation.speech:
Right, so to handle precedence in a single pass, I’d just tweak the ordering of when I apply the operators, but still keep only one running result.

I’d keep `result`, `currentNumber`, and `lastOp`. As I scan, when I hit an operator, I decide whether it’s high or low precedence. If it’s `+` or `-`, I immediately apply it to `result` with `currentNumber`, like before. If it’s `*` or `/`, I don’t need anything special: I just do `result = result * currentNumber` or `result = result / currentNumber` right away. The fact that I’m checking the current operator is enough to enforce precedence, because when I see a `*` or `/`, I compute that before moving on.

So in “3+5*2”, I’d do: see 3, on `+` do `result = 3`; see 5, on `*` do `result = 3*5 = 15`; see 2, end of string, apply `*` again: `result = 15*2 = 30`. Since I’m always applying `*` and `/` as soon as I see them, they naturally get higher precedence than `+` and `-` in this single-pass approach.

I’d just scan the string left to right and whenever I see an opening parenthesis `(`, I’d start a fresh local result and evaluate everything until I hit the matching `)`, but all in the same pass using a single global `result` and `currentNumber`. topic: Find minimum cost path in a 2D grid.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Let's say you have an N x M grid of non-negative costs, and you start at (0,0) and want to reach (N-1,M-1) moving only right or down. How would you compute the minimum cost path, and what time and space complexity would your approach have?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so I’d use dynamic programming. Let dp[i][j] be the minimum cost to reach cell (i, j). The transition is:

dp[i][j] = cost[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1])

with dp[0][0] = cost[0][0], and for the first row/column you can only come from one direction. We fill the table row by row or column by column. That’s O(N*M) time and O(N*M) space. If we want to optimize space, we can keep only one row or one column, bringing space down to O(min(N, M)).

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and spot on. Now, suppose the grid is huge and stored in a file on disk, so you cannot load the entire N x M matrix into memory at once; you can only stream it row by row. How would you adapt your minimum-cost-path solution to work under this memory constraint, and what would the memory usage look like asymptotically?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so since I only get the grid row by row, I’d use the row-based DP optimization. I maintain a 1D array dp of size M, where dp[j] is the min cost to reach column j in the current row.

For the first row, I just do a running sum from left to right. For each new row streamed from disk, I update dp in place: dp[0] += cost[i][0], and for j > 0, dp[j] = cost[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j-1]) where dp[j] is the value from the previous row and dp[j-1] is from the current row. That way I only need O(M) memory, plus O(1) extra.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and exactly what I was looking for. Now, suppose instead of only moving right and down, you are allowed to move in all four directions (up, down, left, right), and costs are still non-negative; how would you find the minimum cost path from (0,0) to (N-1,M-1), and why is your earlier DP approach no longer valid in this setting?

topic: Flatten a binary tree to a linked list.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: How would you flatten a binary tree to a linked list in-place such that the linked list uses the right pointers and follows the preorder traversal of the tree? Please describe both a recursive and an iterative approach and compare their time and space complexities.

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay so we want to modify the tree in-place so that every node’s left becomes null and the right chain is the preorder traversal.

Recursive approach:  
One clean way is a reverse preorder (right, left, root). I keep a global or reference variable `prev = null`. Then I recurse: `flatten(node->right)`, `flatten(node->left)`, and at each node I set `node->right = prev`, `node->left = null`, and update `prev = node`. This effectively stitches the list from the end back to the start. Time is O(n) since we visit each node once, and space is O(h) due to recursion stack (h = tree height; O(n) worst case, O(log n) for balanced).

Iterative approach:  
One iterative method uses a stack. Push the root, then while stack not empty, pop `curr`, push `curr->right` then `curr->left` (so left is processed first), and set `curr->right` to the top of the stack (if any) and `curr->left = null`. That simulates preorder traversal. Time is O(n), space is O(n) in the worst case for the stack.

Alternatively, there’s a Morris-style iterative approach with O(1) extra space: for each node, if it has a left child, find the rightmost node in its left subtree (predecessor), connect `predecessor->right` to `curr->right`, move the left subtree to the right (`curr->right = curr->left`, `curr->left = null`), then move `curr = curr->right`. This is also O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: That was clear and you covered the Morris-style idea nicely. As a follow-up, suppose you are given a very deep, skewed binary tree that can cause stack overflow with recursion; how would you safely implement the flatten operation iteratively without extra asymptotic space (i.e., O(1) auxiliary space), and what invariants would you maintain while transforming the tree?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Hmm, okay, so if the tree is very deep and skewed, the main issue is avoiding recursion because of stack overflow. I’d still use the Morris-style approach I mentioned, but I’d be careful about how I traverse so I don’t rely on any extra containers like an explicit stack.

So my assumption is we just want to keep the traversal preorder while not blowing the call stack. I’d maintain the invariant that at any point, the subtree rooted at the current node has its left side either already moved to the right or still in its original form, and everything strictly to the left of the current node (in preorder) is already flattened into a right-only chain.

Concretely, for each node `curr`, if `curr->left` exists, I find the rightmost node in `curr->left` (its predecessor), link `predecessor->right` to `curr->right`, then set `curr->right = curr->left` and `curr->left = nullptr`. The invariant is: before moving `curr` to `curr->right`, all nodes before `curr` in preorder are already on a single right-linked path, and `curr->left` is always null, so the structure to the left is fully flattened.

conversation.speaker: interviewer
conversation.speech: Your understanding of the Morris-style approach is good, but my earlier question was more about reasoning: after you’ve flattened the tree in-place, how would you prove or argue that the resulting right-pointer chain is exactly the preorder traversal of the original tree and that you haven’t lost or duplicated any nodes during the transformation?

conversation.speaker: interviewee
conversation.speech:
Right, so to argue correctness I’d lean on invariants and a structural view of what we’re doing.

First, no nodes are lost or duplicated: we never allocate or delete nodes, we only rewire pointers. Every reassignment of `right` takes an existing subtree and reattaches it; we don’t skip over any subtree without reattaching it somewhere on the right chain.

Second, for preorder correctness with the Morris-style method: when we’re at `curr` with a left subtree, we find its left subtree’s rightmost node `pred` and do `pred->right = curr->right`, then move `curr->right = curr->left` and `curr->left = null`. This is exactly what preorder wants: visit `curr`, then its entire left subtree, then its right subtree. By splicing the original right subtree to the end of the left subtree, we ensure that, as we keep walking `curr = curr->right`, we’ll traverse `curr`, then all of its left subtree, then all of its original right subtree in that order.

We can formalize it inductively: assume that for all nodes before `curr` in preorder, their subtrees have already been rearranged into correct right-only chains. The transformation at `curr` preserves their order and transforms `curr`’s subtree so that a simple rightward traversal from the root now yields exactly the preorder of the original tree, with every node appearing once.
